entry.title: AI and Value
entry.summary: Watching AI devalue so much around us - we need to change the conversation. Less about how much more we can do, and more about how we can do better – it all depends on what we value.

div.p: I went to a public lecture this week on AI and creativity Future Minds: Creativity and Ethics in the Age of AI hosted by Dr Rebecca Marrone and Dr Maria Vieira. Afterwards, a few work colleagues and I sat around talking about what it all means. We all had backgrounds in creative fields – so the question of what AI means for that world felt pretty immediate. We spoke about friends experiencing a drop-off in work as clients opt for AI-generated work for "free" rather than paying designers. We chatted about the slop and how much of what is generated by AI is just slop. What I kept coming back to was this idea of 'value' – what it is and where in the chain to people place it.

The dominant argument for AI right now is that it's a multiplier – you're 30x more productive, you can output more, faster, and at lower cost. The numbers are always on the positive – it's more of everything. What's conspicuously missing from this argument is any reckoning with what more actually does to value.

We're living through a particular kind of abundance right now – not the abundance anyone was really hoping for where we have more money, free time, freedom, and care, more time and capacity for the things that matter. Instead, we just live in a time of more stuff – more slop, half-arsed attempts, and poor quality. It's fast-fashion logic applied to everything, with social media driving attention and AI the foot on the accelerator. The value of stuff has plummeted to the length of our attention span.

This isn't a new dynamic. Post-war, in an age of genuine scarcity, more really was better. Mass production meant a genuine improvement in people's lives. But the further you go down that road, the more quality tends to dip, because the pressure is to become cheaper and cheaper. The value of what's being produced declines while the volume increases.

You can see it in fashion where a $5 t-shirt now exists – a true marvel of mass production. But what is its value if you don't evaluate the true cost – not at the register, but in the sweatshops full of underpaid workers and the over-farmed fields that yield little but subsistence. You can see it in music where streaming provides access to an almost limitless catalogue of sound, but in doing so devalues our engagement with any of it to fractions of a cent. The art and craft that goes into producing a track, the actual skill required – these things got compressed into a monthly fee that rounds down to nothing for artists, but meanwhile the record labels are still profitable.

Now AI is doing the same thing to the written word, to design, to creative work more broadly. Anecdotal evidence from designers I know suggests that clients are moving toward AI tools and away from commissioning actual designers.

And here's the thing: I think AI could be great at removing the grunt work often involved in design – the high-volume, lower-stakes work needed to produce quality. Good designers have always tried to systematise the repetitive stuff – clipping out product outlines, matching colours across media – so they can spend more time on the work that actually requires thinking. The problem is that we're not using AI to free up that thinking time – the clients are not engaging with designers in the first place. They're using AI to eliminate the design and the thinking altogether - that's not where they see value. They see it as more, more design and for no cost. The race isn't toward better design and higher value work. It's toward more.
If that continues, we reduce everything to nothing until it becomes worthless – and then it gets subsumed by the platforms and corporations that want to monetise the resulting slop.

Thinking this way is a bit depressing, but I don't think this is the end of the story. My feeling is that value tends to be cyclical. When things get so devalued and commoditised, people start seeking variation and difference. You can see it in craft beer, in specialty coffee roasting, in the slow fashion movement – small-batch, high-care products where someone is actually paying attention to quality. The price goes up, but so does the engagement. Coffee stops being a devalued brown drink and becomes something enjoyed, something of a ritual. People start caring about the provenance of the beans, the process, the craft. Value reappears and becomes baked into the product.

Whether that cycle can operate at mass-market scale, I'm not sure. Maybe some things can never return to holding genuine value - but if the pattern is real, then what is devalued now can recover its value, and quality does find an audience.
div.h3: #### What We Should Be Asking For
div.p: What I'd like to see is more discussion about "better" rather than "more". Not "AI lets us produce 10x more content" but "AI lets our writers do better research and produce more nuanced work." Not "AI replaces our designers" but "AI handles the grunt work so our designers can spend more time actually designing." The tools exist to make that argument – the will to make it is missing.

Part of that is on us as consumers – being willing to disengage from algorithmically driven slop and not participate in the mass culture that demands it. It's up to us to call out when things aren't up to scratch and to genuinely value the people who do the hard work of curation – finding good things, sharing them, creating real signal in a sea of noise. In a world of AI-generated abundance, the person who curates well is doing something AI can't: exercising taste, judgement, and care on your behalf. That's worth recognising and supporting.

The harder question is how we collectively calibrate what we value beyond individual spending decisions. Consumer choice matters, but it's not enough on its own – not everyone has the luxury of paying more for the better thing, and the signals we send through the market are blunt instruments at best. We need better ways to express and aggregate what we actually want, beyond next quarter's numbers.

The deeper problem is short-termism. Value is a long-term proposition. It's not about next quarter or next financial year. It's about whether a business – or an industry, or a creative practice – is still standing in five or ten years. The number go up ideology at play that places more value on a rising stock price than anything else is the real problem. It places value only on the short term. It distorts the nature of value altogether.
That's the conversation I'd like to see more of.

entry.title: New Laptop, New Setup
entry.summary: A quick list and quick install of my go-to apps for a new Mac.

div.p: Getting a new work laptop is always a mixed experience. On one hand, new machine. On the other, institutional IT has a habit of locking things down in ways that make setup more of a negotiation than a process. This time around, I have to request admin access to install things, and I only get a 30-minute window to do it in.

So I thought carefully about how to set up my Mac quickly and efficiently. Over time I've evolved a fairly stable list of applications I genuinely depend on, and rather than clicking through installers one by one, I used Homebrew — a command-line package manager that can install applications in bulk. I gave Claude my app list and asked it to generate the Brewfile script to do it, and it worked a treat. Apps are installed - now I just need to log in to everything and set them all up!
Here's the list — my go-to tools for starting up a new Mac.

ul.li: Node - for 11ty / npm projects
NVM – Node version manager
Visual Studio Code – Code editor
Zen Browser – Firefox-based browser with vertical tabs and spaces
Obsidian – Local, Markdown-based knowledge management and note-taking
iA Writer – Distraction-free writing Markdown editor
iA Presenter – Markdown-based presentation tool
Grammarly – Grammar checker
AppCleaner – Thorough app uninstaller
DaisyDisk – Disk space visualiser
CleanShot X – Screenshot and screen recording tool
DeskPad – Virtual display for screen sharing
Thaw – Menu bar manager
Soulver – Notepad calculator
OmniFocus – Task management
WhatCable – Identifies what a USB-C cable can actually do
Handy – Free, open-source offline speech-to-text dictation
MacWhisper – Audio transcription
Brain.fm – Focus music
1Password – Password manager
VLC – Media player
Gifski – Video-to-GIF converter
Dropbox – Cloud storage and file sync

div.p: If you're keen to do this yourself, there's the two files you'll need: Brewfile and Install.sh. You can go ahead and edit these to suit your needs - then just type into the terminal:

entry.title: Obsidian and the Distributed Learning System
entry.summary: A personal learning system built on Obsidian, your own Domain, and ActivityPub Hubs could finally make the Distributed Learning System I sketched in 2017 a buildable reality.

div.p: Back in 2017 I wrote a post called Beyond the LMS that sketched out an idea I called the Distributed Learning System. The core argument was simple: the LMS serves institutions, not learners. It enforces time-boxed access, centralises control, embeds surveillance, and locks students out of their own learning the moment a session ends. The alternative I proposed was a federated model – Nodes and Hubs – where each learner owns and controls their own space, connects to institutional Hubs when needed, and takes everything with them when they leave.
It was speculative at the time, but I think it's becoming buildable now.

The LMS hasn't changed much since 2017, and neither has the underlying problem. It's a system designed around institutional needs: processing grades, managing enrolments, tracking student activity. The learner is a secondary concern – a recipient of content, a submitter of assessments, a data point in an analytics dashboard.

My argument is that it isn't a tool for learning. It doesn't aid learning, not in any real sense; it simply provides an access point to some pretty ordinary tools – discussion boards, content repositories, assignment dropboxes. Things that could be replicated with documents and some cloud storage account. What's missing is any conception of the learner as someone with a continuous, growing body of knowledge that extends beyond a single course, a single session or a single institution. It's not designed for learning, but for administering an educational product.

The LMS frames thinking about learning within the container of a course - a singular site, timeframe, and cohort. But learning doesn't have hard edges. It doesn't stop when the session ends. A student who finishes a subject on organisational behaviour and starts a subject on ethics is still the same person, still building the same understanding. The LMS treats them as two separate events. A genuine learning system would treat them as two moments in a continuous process. A body of knowledge that extends and grows organically.
div.h3: The Node: Obsidian as Personal Learning System
div.p: Over the last couple of years, I've been spending more of my time with Obsidian. And the more I use it, the more I see it as a practical realisation of the Node concept from that 2017 post.

Obsidian is a free, Markdown-based tool that stores files locally and lets you link, tag, and connect ideas into a knowledge graph. Critically, it embodies the principle of file over app – your files are yours, in an open format, readable by any text editor. No database lock-in, no subscription trap, no vendor dependency. I've migrated from Evernote to Ulysses and know exactly what those dependencies cost when you want to leave. Markdown and local files solve that problem.

What's changed my thinking about Obsidian is realising it's not just a writing tool – it's a personal information system. Plugins allow you to fetch data from the web, connect to external services via APIs, and automate workflows using basic JavaScript. I use one that pulls information from IMDB when I log what I'm watching. That same architecture could pull content from a course platform, sync discussion board posts, or receive feedback from a teaching team. The learner interacts only with their own Node – their own environment – and the institutional content comes to them.

This is exactly the model I described in 2017. The difference is that in 2017 I was sketching a system that would need to be built. Obsidian is a system that already exists, with an ecosystem of plugins and an architecture designed to support exactly this kind of extension.

This desire for a personal knowledge system isn't new. Vannevar Bush imagined something like it in 1945 with the Memex — a device that would store all of a person's books, records, and communications, and allow them to trail through that material associatively rather than by fixed index. What Bush was describing was a machine that learned alongside you, accumulating and connecting your intellectual life rather than filing it away. Obsidian is the closest thing to a practical Memex I've encountered – modest in its ambitions, but real and usable today.
div.h3: The Hub: ActivityPub as the Connective Layer
div.p: In the 2017 model, Hubs were the institutional layer – course spaces where Nodes connect, content is distributed, and interactions occur. The Hub establishes the relationship between learners and the institution, defines what data is shared and for how long, and then releases the learner when the course ends – with their own copy of everything.

Mike Caulfield's federated wiki project was an early attempt to build something like this in practice – shared public resources that individuals could fork, annotate, and make their own, while still connecting back to the commons. The personal copy and the shared space coexisted rather than competing.

What makes this more concrete now is ActivityPub. ActivityPub is the open protocol that underpins the fediverse – Mastodon and a growing range of other federated services. It's designed precisely for this: distributed nodes communicating through agreed protocols, without requiring a central authority. A course Hub running on ActivityPub would be a federated space – students subscribe to it from their own Node, receive content and discussion threads, contribute back, and then retain a local copy of everything when the course concludes.

Discussion boards are the obvious starting point. Currently, they're among the most valuable artefacts of a course – spaces where students share resources, build understanding together, and create something with genuine learning value. And then access is revoked. The discussion board gets switched off, and everything in it disappears from the student's world. A federated approach inverts this: the discussion happens in a shared Hub, but each participant's Node pulls down a local copy. The learning stays with the learner.

The same logic applies to course content, feedback, and assessment. Rather than the institution holding everything and granting access on its terms, the learner holds everything and grants the institution access on agreed terms. This is the shift from institutional management to personal ownership that the LMS has never been able to make.

The third layer is the web-facing component – what I'm thinking of as the Domain. Not necessarily a full Domain of One's Own in the original sense, but a web application that sits between the learner's personal Obsidian Node and the institutional Hub. It's the public or semi-public face of the learner's knowledge system: a place to publish, to share selectively, to make certain things visible to the institution for assessment purposes while keeping others private.

Obsidian already supports this through its publish features and, more practically, through plugins that push content to GitHub and generate a static website from your vault. The Domain becomes the learner's outward-facing layer – the interface through which they interact with the institutional Hub, submit work, and optionally share their learning more broadly.

The stack, then, looks like this: Obsidian as the personal Node, a Domain as the web connector, and ActivityPub Hubs as the federated course spaces. Each layer is already buildable with existing tools. What's missing isn't the technology – it's the will to configure it this way, and perhaps a plugin or two to connect the pieces more cleanly.

None of this requires massive infrastructure. We're talking about text files, Markdown, and protocols designed to run on modest hardware. The compute requirements are minimal – no large language models, no sprawling cloud dependencies, nothing that couldn't run on a phone or a basic local machine. Storage scales with what you put in it, and with cloud storage being ubiquitous, it's already in most learners' pockets.

What it does require is a different way of thinking about who the learning system serves. The LMS was built to serve the institution. The Distributed Learning System is built to serve the learner – and to keep serving them after the course ends, after the program concludes, after they've moved on to the next thing. That's what lifelong learning actually requires: not just the aspiration, but the infrastructure.

I've been living with my Personal Learning System for a couple of years now – but it's not connected or distributed. My Obsidian vault is where ideas accumulate, connect, and resurface. Posts from ten years ago link to things I'm thinking about today. Work I did at one institution informs what I'm doing at another. The knowledge doesn't disappear when the context changes – because it lives with me, not with the institution.
I think the pieces are finally here to start building something new!

entry.title: Silhouettes
entry.summary: A silhouette strips away everything that makes us three-dimensional, yet somehow still carries something unmistakably true.

div.p: A while back, I watched the movie Monkey Man and documentary The Mission back-to-back, I found myself connecting them through an unexpected visual thread.

Monkey Man is in the same action-revenge genre as John Wick, but what sets it apart is its setting in India. The cinematography really plays into it, using the lush colours and scenes filled with a visceral sense of smell: dust and smoke, spices and perfume. One sequence is shot almost entirely in silhouette, and it really grabbed me. A good actor brings tonality, structure, and three-dimensionality to a character, yet all of that gets stripped away in a silhouette shot. What remains is shape and outline, and somehow that's enough. The character still lives in it. There's also a puppetry sequence that pushed the same thought further – this ancient art form built entirely from silhouettes, capable of extraordinary detail and dimension through a completely flat, monochromatic language.

The Mission took the idea somewhere else entirely. The documentary follows a missionary who travelled to North Sentinel Island in the Andaman archipelago and was killed by the Sentinelese people shortly after landing. The Indian government has long mandated no contact with the island – the Sentinelese don't seek contact either, don't venture beyond their own waters, and don't invite visitors. What we have of them, as a result, is almost nothing: a handful of zoomed photographs taken from a distance, figures on a beach. Silhouettes on white coral sand.

There is a real inability to describe these as three-dimensional beings. No one knows their names, their culture, what they value or prize. And yet they're clearly people – full and complex lives being lived just out of reach. What we have are these framed shapes, stark against the sand, and that's it.

The connection between the two films clicked into something broader. A silhouette isn't just a visual technique – it's a way of thinking about how we project ourselves, how we're seen, and what we choose to show. We create different silhouettes depending on the medium, the context, the light in which we find ourselves. In some cases the shadow is soft, just a slight blur around the edges – things are visible, but softened, not quite fully real. In other contexts, the shadow is crisp and stark, high definition against its background.

What's interesting is that those silhouettes are still us. They follow the same curves of our bodies. Some bits stick out further than we'd like; others complement us, flattening out the lines and signs of wear. They're roughly our size, our shape, but we can distort them – changing the angle of the light and the plane we project onto, we can appear bigger, taller, tougher than we are in life. The silhouette doesn't show the whites of our eyes, the softness of our palms, our underbelly. It withholds the details that make us vulnerable. But it doesn't stop being us. The representation is still ours, still shaped by us, still carrying something true yet hiding aspects that would make us fully known.

entry.title: My Writing Workflow
entry.summary: Sharing how I am writing posts these days – being open about how I'm using AI to help edit and structure my words but not generate them.

div.p: One of the things that has changed over time is how I approach writing for the blog. I've tried a variety of approaches, partly because writing doesn't come naturally to me – but I value what it does. Getting the ideas out of my head and somewhere else creates space and a sense of mental clarity that's genuinely good for me. That clear space allows me to move on and think about other things rather than replaying the same old loop.

At the very beginning of my blogging life (yes, I still need to migrate my archives across to here), most of what I wrote was essentially automatic writing. Stream of consciousness, write & hit post. The words were sometimes problematic: grammatical errors, spelling mistakes that slipped through. That editorial component of writing is something I've always struggled with. Over time, I've adapted tools to address those shortfalls because I know where my gaps are. While it would be great if this were a collaborative process, I actually enjoy being edited and having another person involved to get feedback on my writing. But I've always wanted blogging to be an independent process and not rely on anyone else, so I've used tools along the way to help fill the gap.

One early adaptation was to speak into my phone instead of typing; then I'd edit the transcript and, through that, develop a blog post. It was faster in some ways, but I didn't enjoy the editing – and that's what I ended up spending all my time on! I started to use Grammarly to help with the editing because it does a great job of all the things beyond spellcheck that I need, and I've stuck as a paid user since[1].

Then I moved to adopting an outlining process for posts, first developing a dot-point structure and coming back to fill in the details. That worked OK, and I still use it, but it lacked the organic feeling I would get from writing automatically or from speaking and transcribing.

I've come back to the transcription method, and a couple of pieces of software have really changed how I work. The is MacWhisper – a relatively inexpensive app that runs a local language model and produces remarkably good transcripts. I've tried most transcription tools as they've come out over the years, and each has had their pros and cons. MacWhisper isn't flawless, but it's pretty close and handles my accent well, manages my tendency to mumble through words. What it does a really good job of is resolving the ambiguity that comes with spoken English – where words sound similar, but only one makes sense in context. The result is still a transcript that needs editing, but the editing is much cleaner – less "what did I actually say here?" and more straightforward editorial work.

Most recently, I've added Claude to the mix – not for generating posts, but for the editorial pass. There is news this week from Anthropic about adding a watermark to text generated by the tool, which is technically quite interesting, but it's also caused quite a stir. I'm not sure if or when the tools to detect its use will arrive, but I thought I would be open about it and share my experience and how I am using the tool.
So my workflow is pretty much the same:

ul.li: I usually start in Just Press Record recording me speaking through my ideas. It saves an audio file from whichever device I'm on to my iCloud account.
Then I drag the audio file onto MacWhisper and generate the transcript.

Then it's over to Claude where I use some basic prompts aimed at cleaning up my verbal tics and developing a structure. Typically it's something like: Here's a transcript, here's roughly what I covered and the main point I want to get across, clean up the structure, condense the parts where I ramble. It gives me back my words in a more coherent form and structure.

Then I copy that and head over to Obsidian. It's here that I read through the post and edit as I go. There are some LLM tics that I hate – I never liked 'em' dashes, however I love dash-based punctuation, but my tool of choice is the lesser-known 'en' dash. Grammarly is also involved, and it tends to push sentence structure to a more simplified approach – which is in keeping with my 'style' (FYI it did not like that last sentence at all!). I'm accepting and rejecting suggestions, adding and rewriting sentences and occasionally whole paragraphs. And somewhere towards the end there is a post that I'm happy with.

I then copy the file over to the blog site in Visual Studio Code, run the build script to check for errors, and if it's good, I push it to GitHub, which builds the site and serves it on GitHub Pages and pushes shared posts to Mastodon and Bluesky.

div.p: There are a few steps in there and a bunch of tools. But for me, they each serve a specific purpose and role. Throughout all of this – these remain my ideas. The words, well, they've changed and evolved throughout the entire process. What I feel makes them mine is hitting that publish button and taking responsibility for them being in the world.

For me, the role of the LLM, the AI, isn't present in the idea, and it's not in the words themselves. I assume that a watermark may say differently – but I do wonder if a pass through an LLM means that the content was in any way AI-generated. I think that distinction matters. There wasn't a prompt: write a blog post about this topic. The use of an LLM was a single step in a broader process: "Here is a blog post I've already spoken; now help me with the formatting and structure I haven't had time to do." For me, the LLM has a distinct value proposition, and it plays to what these tools are actually good at – processing text, applying pattern recognition and finding structural inconsistencies. And these are genuinely things that are not a strength of mine.

I can understand those out there who write, and many who write for a living, who find the use of LLMs abhorrent. I do find the generative use of LLMs quite problematic, and the output to be mostly just shit. But I don't feel my use falls into that same basket. The LLM is used as step in a feedback loop – it gives me something to work from, not start with. It's not a replacement for my own judgement, and I never intend to outsource that.
It's still me clicking the buttons and making decisions throughout the process. It's still my words, processed and refined yes, but still mine.

li.p: Somewhat reluctantly! If anyone has suggestions for cheaper or better alternatives, please let me know!! ↩︎

entry.title: AI as Translator
entry.summary: AI as a translation layer unlocks access to things that were previously off-limits. Access isn't the same as mastery, but the empowerment that comes from going further than you could before is real and worth taking seriously.

div.p: Last year we travelled to Japan, and one of the things that had always quietly worried me about travelling in Asia was the language barrier. Not the speaking, that's something I'm familiar with, but the symbol-based written language. Not having an alphabet you recognise to sound out words is really disorientating. Not being able to even make an educated guess or embarrassing attempt at a word was really outside my comfort zone. That said, I was so keen to see Japan I couldn't let that stop me (and the family) from having an amazing holiday.

I made sure we had mobile data before we left, specifically so we could lean on translation tools if and when we needed them. In our travels, we ended up in a few places where very little was in English – menus, signs, instructions – and being able to point a phone camera at something and get a live translation on screen unlocked experiences that would otherwise have stayed closed. It wasn't perfect. A lot of it ended up being hints rather than translations — which was fine and an acceptable limitation. Those familiar will know that language doesn't translate directly anyway. Slang, jokes, wordplay – these exist in every language and can't just be converted. But good enough was genuinely good enough. It meant we could venture outside the tourist bubble, into places that don't see many Western visitors. And there's a particular thrill to that kind of experience, as it unlocked something special and unique.
That feeling kept coming back to me when I started thinking about AI and vibe coding. Why had so many people got enraptured by it?

Vibe coding is using AI as a translation layer. You speak in plain language, and you get a working application of the thing you described. For someone who isn't a programmer, that's magic! It's the same kind of unlocking I felt in Japan. Something that was previously off-limits becomes accessible. You're not fluent – and you know you're not fluent – but you can go further than you could before, and that's intoxicating in its own right. You don't know the code or the language - but that wasn't the point. The point was to unlock what was inaccessible before.

I learned Swedish in a previous life, which gave me an appreciation for what fluency actually means. Watching Swedish films with subtitles, I noticed the best translators weren't translating words – they were translating the context. They wouldn't just take a literal translation of the joke, they'd rewrite it into a joke that worked in the context of the new language. That was the skill of the translator – the real expertise was in meaning, not the text. That's what a fluent programmer does too: they don't just write code, they think about it in a context that goes well beyond a literal translation. How will this affect other functions and processes? How will this affect performance and memory allocation? How does this protect data and access? AI doesn't replicate that level of expertise. But for someone who has never had access to that language at all, even an imperfect translation opens doors that were previously shut.

I was reading Darcy Norman's recent post on the anthropomorphisation of AI. I'm very sceptical and concerned about that framing of AI, turning a tool into a person and imbuing it with personality. But I think it's pointing at something real. That kind of psychology isn't really about the AI feeling human; it's really about the user feeling empowered. We personify it because it gives us something we are grateful for. That's the thing worth understanding. People have always done this with their tools - naming the truck or their tools, giving it a personality and imbuing it with characteristics and traits. That desire comes from how the tool makes us feel.

The best examples of vibe coding I've come across aren't about making money or disrupting industries. They're about someone building a small tool that lives on their desktop and does the specific thing they've always needed done – something that would have taken hours of repetitive work, now available as a command. That's not a trivial thing. It shifts time and attention from low-value execution to higher-value decision-making. It's the same freedom we felt in Japan when we stopped worrying about language and could just enjoy being somewhere new. We didn't need to concern ourselves with decoding the symbols on a menu, but instead concentrate on the actual experience of being somewhere new and trying something we'd never tried before.

The limitations are real and worth naming. I wouldn't replace a skilled translator with Google Translate, and I wouldn't replace experienced engineers with AI-generated code for anything that matters at scale. But there's a genuine and distinct value in the vibe coder – the person who can now make something they couldn't before, even imperfectly, even with full awareness of the constraints. Access isn't the same as mastery, but access is still worth something.

entry.title: The Binaries of Education
entry.summary: In education, context determines what works – not ideology.

div.p: In such a contested space as education, there are bound to be arguments that arise. I’ve occasionally engaged in these arguments, feeling strongly enough to pick a side and contribute - throwing a few strong words out into the ether. Most of those debates have fizzled out over time despite their original fervour and passion. I've also seen some notable grudges form when combatants adopt a never-forgive, never-forget attitude.

What I see as the common element in these arguments is that critical issues boil down to a binary point of contention. I’ve opted out of engaging in much of the "scholarship in education" (specifically the academic publishing and ego-driven influence world) because the binary always comes down to a belief in a right and a wrong way of doing something.

I’m more of a Por qué no los dos? kind of guy and that’s because my experience in education to span beyond a single context. What tends to undermine every right/wrong and good/bad binary I’ve encountered is that there’s a specific context where something either works or breaks. And that experience in that context then informs a worldview and perspective moving forward.

Working in a professional context in higher education I have always worked outside the context of faculties, faculty and academia. My relationships and partnerships in the work I do have always spanned those contexts - I work across disciplines, levels, reputations, experience. I’ve never been pigeonholed into a discipline, a mode of teaching, a technology, a pedgogy, or a practice. I’ve worked across them all, seen many of them work and seen them break when applied to different contexts. A technology that improves learning in one context will negate learning in another. A didactic approach works in one context but not another. Neither is fundamentally wrong or right – instead, it is the context that dictates the appropriateness. There are pros and cons, levels of rightness and wrongness - but in the end, context matters. Technology is just a tool until it is weaponised and used to inflict harm.

What I’ve found in educational circles is that, too often, binaries move towards ideology, which is acted on with religious fervour. There is only one true way of doing and seeing things. That two concepts cannot be of equal measure and contain their own pros AND cons. Everything else is wrong because this is the right way to do it.

The cost of this approach is that we lose sight of the bigger picture. We lose common ground, connection becomes harder and harder, and we become disconnected islands with a gulf between us. I would rather we become more pluralistic and accepting of difference – that we act within our contexts rather than judge others for theirs. There is a growing need for pluralism, for accepting that difference is not a problem to solve but rather a distinct advantage. We are better when we operate beyond the binaries and seek to connect with others rather than push them apart.

entry.title: Innovation without solving problems
entry.summary: Is AI an attempt to take the Rot Economy to its illogical conclusion? Can you maximise profit without solving a problem and without a quality product or user experience?

div.p: Ed Zitron has been on a tear over the last year. His newsletter and podcast Better Offline make a sustained and uncomfortable argument about what has gone wrong inside the world's largest technology companies. Ed has spent a lot of time recently on AI, but I really vibed with his earlier critique. The Rot Economy: a philosophy – or perhaps an ideology – where the pursuit of endless growth has been prioritised over product quality, user experience, and the original purpose that made these companies worth using in the first place. Loyal users have been left behind. Products have gotten worse. And the people running these companies have gotten richer.
I think he's right. And I think it connects to something I've been turning over for a while about what innovation actually means.

Real innovation requires two things: change and a problem worth solving. Not a manufactured problem, not a financial problem, not a problem that exists only because venture capital needs a 10x return – a real problem, felt by real people. When you strip that requirement away, what you're left with isn't innovation. It's solutionism. The answer that goes looking for a question.

That's where I land on generative AI. I genuinely struggle to identify the problem it solves. What is the problem that it actually solves? What it has identified is a gap in the investment landscape – a place to park capital in search of returns that have become harder to find as big tech has consolidated its dominance. Rather than address the structural conditions that make those returns scarce, the money has moved sideways into the next technical novelty. Generative AI is not a response to a need.
The pattern isn't new, though. We've watched it play out already – just more slowly.

Facebook, in its early years, had genuine value. It solved a real problem: staying connected with people across distance. Before the ads, before the algorithm, before the growth imperative took hold, there was something real happening – a sense of everyday connection, of living vicariously through the small moments of people you cared about. That was worth something.

Then the model changed. Growth became the only metric that mattered. Ads appeared, then multiplied. The algorithm began promoting engagement over connection, which in practice meant conflict, outrage, and sensation over the quiet updates that made the thing useful in the first place. The ratio of ads to genuine posts inverted until the product became effectively unusable. For every post from a friend, fifteen ads. And because there are fifteen ads, there are fewer posts from friends. So it fills the gap with recommended posts from strangers or ads pretending to be strangers.

Twitter followed the same arc. When it was less focused on profit, it was a genuinely useful place – democratic in a way that felt new, allowing anyone to reach anyone. As commercial pressure intensified, moderation loosened, algorithms promoted the most inflammatory content, and the platform became a place where discourse goes to die rather than happen.

This is what the Rot Economy looks like in practice. It's not a sudden collapse. It's a slow hollowing out – the original value gradually replaced by the mechanisms of extraction, until the host has nothing left to give. Which, as Zitron puts it, is parasitic behaviour. And a parasite that kills its host has nowhere left to go.

AI is the Rot Economy taken to its logical conclusion. It doesn't just hollow out an existing product — it attempts to bypass the problem/product paradigm altogether. In the context of global climate change, the investment in data centres to run AI far exceeds that of installing renewable energy and electrifying everything, which seems absolutely insane. Yet here we are.

And while we're doing that, the climate crisis continues. The world's most significant and most tractable problem – the one that stands to affect every person, every system, every economy on the planet – sits underfunded and under-prioritised. Instead, we're building infrastructure that consumes more energy, water, and other resources to automate the generation of content that doesn't need to exist. It is hard to think of a more complete misdirection of talent and capital. What if the hundreds of billions of dollars pledged to build data centres were spent electrifying the nation with renewables?

The problem is that "number go up" has become so synonymous with success that we've stopped asking what the number is actually measuring. Growth is a metric, not a purpose. You can have billions of users engaging with something less, because it works better and asks less of them. That's a different business model, yes – but so much of the current model is so fundamentally broken that rewriting it isn't a threat, it's an opportunity.

What we actually need is less. Simpler. More federated, more cooperative, more focused on doing fewer things well. Technology that reduces its footprint rather than expanding it. Innovation that starts with the problem rather than the return. The tools exist. The knowledge exists. What's missing is the will to point them at something that matters. Number go up, until it doesn't. The question is what we've built by the time it stops.

entry.title: Intentional Engagement
entry.summary: I'm trying to change how I engage with technology – to move past ubiquity and towards intentionality.

div.p: Twenty-five years of working professionally in and around technology gives you a particular vantage point. The evolution of digital technology over that time has been dramatic: from the hardware evolution of desktop to laptop to mobile, through the dial-up, broadband, fibre, and mobile data eras, through the rise and slow collapse of social media. What I've seen throughout this evolution of technology is how it has moved from something you had to seek out to something that now seeks you out.

The technology of the early 2000s was full of friction. There was time and space involved, as well as a level of knowledge and skill required to engage. You went to a specific device in a specific room. You couldn't just go online – you had to dial up, viscerally and aurally. You couldn't just post something; you had to write, edit, code, FTP, and break, check and fix. Everything related to digital technology required an intention because it was slow and complicated to use.

What has changed over time is that friction has been reduced. The digital technologies we have today have become so frictionless, ubiquitous, and embedded in every aspect of life that they've become second nature – and, in doing so, they've quietly removed the need to make decisions. Rather than living in the moment, we pull out our phones to record life as it passes by. The technology is available wherever and whenever we are, without ever having to ask if we want it there. It's enmeshed in our routines, a crutch we lean on to get through the day. To feed us information, show us the way, connect with others, and get lost in the endless flow of the Stream.

The Stream was the right way to think about what we experience online – Mike Caulfield named it well. But over the last several years it has become so swollen with disinformation, misinformation, and noise that it's now the Torrent. You cannot help but get swept away by it. And in the tumult, we lose ourselves and each other – our spaces, places, and communities. The spaces we once shared have been commercialised and algorithmically flooded, and there doesn't seem to be a safe place left. The Torrent swept away the town square and swallowed the commons.

We've gone from being locked out because of the complexity and intentionality required to engage, to being trapped by ubiquity and the Torrent's insistence that we voice every opinion, contribute every thought, broadcast our most unfiltered selves. To be a content creator! To throw another take into the outrage machine!

The deeper problem with the Torrent isn't just the noise. It's that the algorithm replaced intention with compulsion – and in doing so, it removed something we've barely noticed we've lost: the ability to choose.

Think about what browsing used to mean. Channel surfing. Wandering through a record shop. Pulling a book off a shelf because the spine caught your eye. Dipping in, skipping past, lingering somewhere unexpected. These were intentional acts of exploration, guided by curiosity rather than by a system optimised to keep you watching.

Streaming services don't let you channel surf. Social media feeds don't let you wander. They push, and the algorithm decides what you see, in what order, for how long, and what comes next. You live in a world without meaningful choices, even as the illusion of infinite choice surrounds you. The recommendation engine isn't serving your curiosity. It's serving your attention to someone else's commercial interests.

The contrast is clearest when you compare something like Mastodon to Instagram. On Mastodon, you follow people deliberately, you see what they post in the order they posted it, and nothing is trying to hijack your attention beyond that. It's quiet. It requires a little effort. It feels, in the best sense, old-fashioned – like a space you inhabit rather than a current that carries you. Instagram, by contrast, is pure algorithm. What you see is determined not by who you chose to follow but by what Meta has calculated will keep you scrolling. Your choices are largely decorative.
Except when we switch off.

Then we get silence. Unnerving at first, nothing but the sounds of the place you thought you'd lost. The breeze, the trees, the birds – they're still there. So is the neighbour with their leaf blower. But it's here that we can find solace. We can rest and recover and start anew from this place.

This is what intentional spaces look like, and what we've lost so much of. Not necessarily new tools or different platforms, but the capacity to engage on our own terms – to seek rather than be served, to choose rather than be chosen for.

What I've started doing instead is tending my own space. It might be a domain – a website, but I prefer to think of it as a garden – something organic, with room to grow and change, intentionally mine. It feels like coming home, or coming full circle.

Intent, in this sense, is the opposite of getting lost in the Torrent. It's about finding myself and finding others. It's antithetical to the algorithm – it's about wandering, making records of what I find, seeking connection rather than having connection served to me. It means going at my own pace, writing the code that underpins the site, matching the specifics of my needs rather than fitting myself to a platform. The site isn't finished and probably never will be. But that's the point. A garden grows.

The connections to the world still matter. My feelings on global politics change nothing, but my connections to people and places around the world do. They are the strings worth pulling on – things that link me to something bigger than my local geography. The intent is to nurture those connections deliberately, rather than have them mediated and monetised by systems that benefit from keeping me agitated.

What's missing, broadly, are the spaces we used to have for connecting – both physical and virtual – that operated at human scale, without an algorithm deciding who gets to speak and who gets amplified. Building those back, or finding the ones that still exist, is slow work. It means fighting the pull of the Torrent. But occasionally you find others doing the same thing, moving in roughly the same direction, and for a moment the current doesn't feel quite so strong.
Intent isn't a rejection of technology. It's a reclamation of why we wanted it in the first place.

entry.title: Simultaneous Monologues
entry.summary: Some thoughts on online dialogue and debate.

div.p: Social media and media in general promote the idea that they create dialogue around big issues. But this doesn't resonate with me, because what I see isn't dialogue at all. There's no free-speaking – what we see is edited, controlled, asynchronous snippets that remove the context of time and space. It's not a conversation or discussion because there is no central point of meeting or exchange, no rules of engagement, no shared sense of what the topic actually is. And there's no real purpose either – no aim to the conversation, just a mechanism for attracting attention and driving people toward more ads.

What happens in these media spaces isn't dialogue or debate. A debate has parameters, purpose, and a premise. These things allow arguments to be formed, compared, and contrasted. They allow logic to be applied.

What media does is hijack the concepts of human interaction and subvert them. Rather than dialogue, it creates a place for simultaneous monologues – each voice its own star – and then turns up the volume. In many ways, media behaves as a pyromaniac would: stacking the fuel, igniting the flame, and standing back as it all burns, enraptured by the chaos, with no concern for the results. And because there are no physical consequences, it just moves on to the next thing. And the next. And the next. Without any purpose beyond the gratification of creating a frenzied moment.

The web is capable of dialogue, yes, but not at scale. Dialogue is of human scale – not machines, not networks, but direct and tied. And it isn't only a space for airing disagreements. More often than not, dialogue requires some baseline of shared understanding to function at all: boundaries, rules, and conventions – perhaps unspoken, but mutual. That kind of mutuality can only happen at human scale.

For all the talk about the town square, we must remember that the square was not the place of debate or dialogue, but a space for shouting at one another from our own soapboxes. Dialogue has its home in cozy bars and cafes, on sofas and lounges, on long walks or seated around the fire – in shared places. Perhaps we never needed the town square online. What we need is something more akin to those cozy spaces.

entry.title: From Waterfall to Snowball
entry.summary: Or how I learnt to stop fighting complexity and learned to work with it.

div.p: This is another post in my series on shared solutions – things I've done to solve problems, the approaches taken, and what actually worked. Early in my career I was doing production work, operating within systems. That's complicated territory: lots of moving parts, but ultimately knowable and manageable with the right expertise.

The shift came when I moved into designing systems rather than running them. Suddenly I wasn't just dealing with tasks and processes – I was dealing with people, infrastructure, workflows, competing priorities, and stakeholders who all had different expectations. The inputs multiplied. The interactions between those inputs became unpredictable. That's complexity, and it requires a fundamentally different way of working.

One of the ideas that has most shaped how I work is the Cynefin framework – specifically the distinction between complicated and complex problem spaces. Once I learnt how to spot the difference, things fell into place in terms of how I needed to work in them.

The problem was that the institutions I have worked in still haven't made that distinction. The clearest example was a project I worked on that was run under PRINCE2 – a project methodology the university had signed itself up to. PRINCE2 has its merits, particularly in terms of accountability. But it locked us into a rigidly linear way of working that wasn't suited to what we were actually doing.

We went over time. We went over budget. We delivered something in the end, but the process was painful, and the outcome was compromised. And the culprit, more than anything else, was the assumption that you could plan everything upfront and execute sequentially – that the path from A to B was knowable before you started walking it.
After that, I made a commitment to do things differently.

After that project, I stumbled into the Lean Startup model and its Build-Measure-Learn cycle. It's deceptively simple, but it reframes everything. You do something, measure what happened, learn from it, and build again. You don't try to have the fully formed answer before you start. You start with a sketch and add fidelity as you go.

This mapped naturally onto the practice I was already familiar with - it's how design works. Pencil sketches first, then more detail, then more detail again. You introduce new elements, encounter new constraints, better understand context, and adapt. The solution evolves through the process rather than being designed before it begins. Design is the process.

Over the next few projects, I started adapting them to work this way and demonstrated that it worked – delivering on time and on budget. I was also capable of doing something no project had been able to do before - pivot quickly when things changed. The institutional recognition wasn't there, but the results were, and I knew I was on to something.

When I got to Adelaide, the iterative approach wasn't just my personal preference – it became a shared philosophy for the team. Most of the team came from design backgrounds where cycles and iterations were already the norm, which made it easier to establish from the start.
What I wanted to articulate – and what eventually became a shorthand for how we talked about our work – was the difference between waterfall and snowball.

Waterfall is the Gantt chart model: stage gates, sequential phases, everything planned upfront and executed in order. Snowball is different. You start with the core concept – the essential idea of what you're trying to do – and you build fidelity through cycles. Each pass adds more detail, more specificity, more refinement. The thing grows as you work on it, shaped by what you learn along the way.

For course design, this looked like: defining the core learning experience we're trying to create. Asking: What do students need to be able to do? What are the outcomes? Then we built on that. Topics, sequence, and activities were worked out iteratively — understanding the whole first, then adding detail in the order that made sense, rather than sequentially.
Working with partners who were using a waterfall approach while we were using a snowball approach made the difference obvious. One model kept hitting walls. The other didn't have the same problems.

Over time, some things did become systematised. Certain approaches got templated. Consistency was developed in the areas where possible. And that consistency freed up energy to focus attention to where it was needed and the parts that couldn't be systematised – usually the people. Freeing up time to spend with people, working with them and developing with them became the secret to success.
But the single most powerful tool in working this way was the retrospective.

Once you've done something, you need to stop and work out what you'll do and not do moving forward. That sounds simple. In practice, it's confronting – it requires honest assessment of what didn't work, which isn't always comfortable. But running retrospectives as a regular ceremony, not a one-off event, trained the team to work that way. They learnt how to give constructive feedback. They learnt to critique the work rather than attack the people. They get better at seeing what actually happened rather than what they hoped would happen.
The retrospective became a cornerstone of how the team operated. It was the mechanism that made the build-measure-learn cycle real rather than theoretical.
div.h3: What Working in Complexity Actually Means
div.p: The underlying insight across all of this is that complexity doesn't reward linear planning. There are too many stakeholders, too many forces at play, too many interactions between parts of the system that you can't anticipate in advance. You can't plan your way through it. You have to build your way through it.

That means accepting that you'll get things wrong. The goal isn't to be right – it's to get things right over time, through cycles of building, measuring, and learning. It means the team has to adapt alongside the work, not just the process itself. And it means treating feedback not as a disruption to the plan, but as the mechanism by which the plan improves.

Having a team that can adapt as a whole to a changing, complex environment is something organisations struggle with, even if they don't recognise it. The solution isn't to solve it with another complicated process, tool, or workflow. The solution is in adapting the process itself and working in a different way - one that is capable of iteration, feedback and learning. If the process cannot learn and adapt, it is doomed in a complex environment. If the team isn't given the chance to learn or adapt either, then you'll quickly lose them too.

entry.title: The Network Should Be Ours
entry.summary: We're living in a world where the service and the product are two completely separate things. What we see are systems corrupted, eroded, and devalued to the extent that we can't trust them.

div.p: After reading an interview with danah boyd on parasocial networks, it got me thinking about a distinction I keep coming back to: the difference between the service and the product:

ul.li: The service is the value proposition, why people show up.
The product is what's actually being sold, where the money actually comes from.

div.p: In a ye'olde world of commerce, these two things used to be the same. A stallholder attracted customers with their fair-priced fresh produce, and people paid a fair price for fresh produce. As businesses evolved, we realised we could abstract away from the connection between the two. In most big businesses today, these two things aren't the same. And nowhere is that more obvious than in social networks.

Take Instagram or Facebook. The service – the reason people signed up – is for social connection. Staying in touch with friends and family, getting a glimpse of what people are up to, that incidental sharing turns out to matter more than we'd admit. The product, though, is an advertising platform. A highly targeted one, because you've handed over enormous amounts of personal information in exchange for the service.

This isn't new. Broadcast television offered entertainment and news as the service, and sold advertising as the product. Newspapers offered a chronicle of the world and sold eyeballs to advertisers too. The difference with social networks is the precision of targeting and the fact that the confusion between service and product has become harder to ignore. When a third of what you see in your feed is an ad, the service starts to degrade noticeably.

We're at a point where that degradation is real enough that people are looking for alternatives. The platforms have become so ravenously commercial that the experience itself is suffering. And yet leaving is hard, because the network has value. Meta has been around long enough, and its networks have grown deep enough, that in many communities and cultures it simply is the infrastructure. I haven't been on Instagram for years and I genuinely feel the absence – not of the platform, but of the incidental social layer it provides.

That's the crux of it. Networks become valuable because they are networks. And at the point where a network becomes infrastructure – where communities genuinely depend on it to function – the question of who owns it starts to matter a great deal.

Right now the answer is: private companies, running for profit, on servers they own, subject to the commercial imperatives of their investors. Governments aren't much better – most of them have outsourced their own digital infrastructure to AWS and equivalent cloud providers, which is a strange position for entities that like to talk about national sovereignty and security.

The advertising model exists partly because of an assumption that people won't pay for these services. That assumption is starting to look shaky – subscription-based media has proven there's a viable user-pays model, at least at the level of survival. But survival isn't the same as the year-on-year growth that keeps investors interested. And so the advertising model persists, because it's the one that scales to the returns investors expect.

The result is that we've built communities on infrastructure that serves different masters than the communities themselves. The platform optimises for engagement and ad revenue. The community needs reliable, trustworthy communication. Those two things are increasingly in conflict.
div.h3: What Community Infrastructure Could Look Like
div.p: What I'd like to advocate for is publicly owned digital infrastructure – local, communal, scaled to the communities it serves.

Think about what community sports teams invest in private digital infrastructure right now. The soccer club my daughter joined ran almost entirely on Facebook – training schedules, game updates, last-minute changes. Not because anyone chose Facebook as the ideal tool, but because it was where everyone already was and there was nothing else. That dependency on a private platform, for something as straightforward as coordinating a kids' football team, points to a real gap.

Local councils and local governments could fill that gap. Running servers and services at community scale keeps people employed, keeps data sovereign, and keeps the service actually oriented toward the community rather than toward advertisers. Yes, it costs more per user than a giant data centre. But that cost is partly the cost of employing someone – and there's value in that beyond the balance sheet.

The Trump era made visible what was always true: centralising so much of our digital life on US-based private services carries real risk. Europe has started responding to this, with moves toward public cloud infrastructure and digital sovereignty. I haven't seen even the beginning of that conversation in Australia.
One more thing worth pulling out. Among the services that have been lost or degraded in the shift to commercial platforms is something that sounds old-fashioned but matters: the chronicle.

Newspapers did something valuable – someone was paid to record the life and times of a community, a role that came with respect and purpose. The value of that work wasn't always immediate – often the real value is in the archives, only becoming clear much later, when someone goes looking for how things changed, how decisions were made, how a community evolved over time. We don't have great ways of seeing change as it happens. The chronicle is one of them.

Social networks, at their best, did something similar – created a record of connection and community that had real value. The problem is that record is held privately, monetised commercially, and could disappear tomorrow if the business model changes.

If communities owned their own infrastructure, they'd own that record too. The network itself – the ability to form connections, build sub-networks, coordinate across geography – would be the service. And the service and the product would, for once, be the same thing.

We could return to the days when the service and the product are one and the same. The thing is, we need to accept the cost and be willing to pay for it. I like the idea of public infrastructure – paying through our taxes so we don't pay for someone else to profit.

entry.title: Tooting from the Blog
entry.summary: My approach to sharing via the fediverse has had to change with the closure of Echofeed. So here's my approach to replacing EchoFeed with a GitHub Action.

div.p: I've been using EchoFeed to crosspost from my blog to Mastodon for a while now. It's a solid little tool, but I've been slack and have been relying on someone else's free hosted service to keep my POSSE workflow running. I'm a massive fan of Robb and have been so appreciative of this tool, which came along at exactly the right time for me. But someone's generosity often hides the amount of effort that goes into it, and now it's been shuttered I need to look for a new solution. Thanks Robb for all the work that you've put into this service and the value it's given my tiny little corner of the web.

With the news, I decided I needed to replace what Echofeed provided - posting to Mastodon is literally the only promotion I do for the site- and rather than migrate to another third-party service, I wondered if I could just use my existing stack instead. The result is a GitHub Action that reads my blog's RSS feed, works out which posts haven't been shared yet, and toots the new ones to Mastodon. I've set it up to also post to Bluesky as well. It runs as part of your existing deployment pipeline, keeps its own state in a JSON file committed to the repo, and requires no server, database, or any other subscription.

blockquote.p: Note: This was vibe-coded with Claude. While I appreciate the craft that goes into coding, I am not blessed with that skill. I know my way around web systems well enough to know what's possible - I just can't make the magic happen. If this puts you off - that's fine. If it inspires you to write something yourself - let me know. I'd be more than happy to swap out the AI slop with something hand-crafted.

div.p: Three pieces:

ul.li: A state file (data/posted-guids.json) that records which feed items have already been posted, so nothing gets duplicated.
A script that fetches the feed, compares it against that state file, and posts anything new to Mastodon's API.
A workflow that runs the script, either on a schedule or as a step in your existing build and deploy pipeline.

div.p: On the very first run, it records everything currently in your feed as "already posted" without tooting any of it. That matters, otherwise your entire back catalogue lands on Mastodon in one go the moment you turn this on. From then on, only genuinely new items get posted.

This is Node, using rss-parser to handle the feed and the built-in fetch for talking to both platforms' APIs. Each post gets a fixed prefix and the title, the feed's <summary> (Mastodon only, see below), the link, and hashtags built from any <category> elements on the item. If the item has an enclosure or <media:content> image, it downloads that once and attaches it natively wherever it's needed, rather than just linking to it.
Mastodon and Bluesky post independently of each other. If one fails, the other still goes out, and only the failed one is retried on the next run.
You can check out the script on GitHub.
Hashtags come from RSS's own <category> element, which rss-parser already collects into item.categories with no extra parsing needed. Add a field to a post's front matter:

pre.code: --- title: All in the Verbs date: 2026-04-10 mastodonTags: [ai, learningdesign] ---

div.p: Keeping it a separate field from whatever tags your site already uses for its own taxonomy or nav matters, since those often include values like "posts" or "nav" you wouldn't want turning into hashtags. Then in the feed template:

Since it's a plain loop over an optional array, posts without mastodonTags just emit zero <category> tags, no conditional needed. A post with [ai, learningdesign] in front matter comes out as #Ai #LearningDesign in the toot.
If you already build and deploy your site through a GitHub Actions workflow as I do, you can fold this in as a second job instead, gated with needs: so it only runs after a successful deploy:

pre.code:
toot: needs: deploy if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && success() runs-on: ubuntu-22.04 permissions: contents: write steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: "24"
- name: Wait for Pages CDN to catch up run: sleep 60 # The deploy job just pushed to gh-pages, but GitHub's CDN can take # a short while to actually serve the new content. Without this, # the feed fetch below can occasionally hit a stale cached version # of feed.xml, missing whatever changed in the most recent deploy.
- name: Install dependencies run: npm install rss-parser
- name: Check feed and post new items env: FEED_URL: ${{ vars.FEED_URL }} MASTODON_INSTANCE_URL: ${{ vars.MASTODON_INSTANCE_URL }} MASTODON_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.MASTODON_TOKEN }} BLUESKY_HANDLE: ${{ vars.BLUESKY_HANDLE }} BLUESKY_APP_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.BLUESKY_APP_PASSWORD }} run: node scripts/toot-new-posts.mjs
- name: Commit updated state file run: | git config user.name "github-actions[bot]" git config user.email "github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com" git add data/posted-guids.json git diff --staged --quiet || git commit -m "Update posted-guids state [skip ci]" git push

div.p: If you want, you could run this as a standalone version that polls every 30 minutes, independent of however your site actually gets built and deployed. That might be useful for you, but that doesn't suit the light touch workflow I have on my personal blog.

ol.li: Get a Mastodon access token. Settings → Development → New Application on your instance, tick write:statuses, create it, copy the token.
Add the two files to your repo: scripts/toot-new-posts.mjs and an empty data/posted-guids.json containing just [], both at the repo root, plus whichever workflow file fits your setup.
Add repo secrets and variables (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions): secret MASTODON_TOKEN, and variables FEED_URL and MASTODON_INSTANCE_URL.
Push, and check the Actions tab. The first run should complete without posting anything, just seeding the state file with your existing posts.
Publish something new to confirm it actually toots.

div.p: If you want a different post format, hashtags, a different field from the feed, whatever, it's all in buildStatusText(). That's the only function you'd realistically need to touch.
Bluesky (AT Protocol) is a different enough API that it's worth knowing the gaps before turning it on:

ul.li: Auth is a handle + app password, not a static token. Generate one in Bluesky's Settings → App Passwords (not your main login password), and the script exchanges it for a short-lived session at the start of each run.

300 characters, not ~500. There isn't room for title, link, hashtags, and a summary, so the Bluesky post drops the summary entirely and just sends the prefix, title, link, and hashtags. If the title alone is long, it's truncated with an ellipsis so the link and hashtags always survive intact.
Links and hashtags need "facets." Unlike Mastodon, having a URL or #tag in the text doesn't make it clickable or searchable, AT Protocol needs an explicit byte-range annotation pointing at each one.
Images upload through a different endpoint (a blob upload, not a multipart form), producing a blob reference rather than a media ID.

div.p: It's genuinely optional. Without both BLUESKY_HANDLE and BLUESKY_APP_PASSWORD set, Bluesky posting is skipped entirely and Mastodon behaves exactly as before. Turn it on later and it gets its own silent first-run seed, same as Mastodon did, so it won't try to post your whole archive the moment it's switched on. State entries are tracked per platform (mastodon:<id>, bluesky:<id>), so a failure on one never causes a duplicate or a skip on the other.
div.h2: One gotcha: give your feed items a stable guid
div.p: The script tells "already posted" from "new" using each item's guid, falling back to its link if the feed doesn't set one:

If your feed template doesn't set an explicit <guid>, most static site generators fall back to using the post's URL as the guid too, which is fine right up until that URL changes. Fix a typo in a slug, correct a post's date, move it between folders, and the URL changes, which means the script sees a "new" item it's never encountered before and toots it again, even though nothing about the content actually changed. I hit exactly this: correcting a post's date shifted its permalink by one day, and the next deploy dutifully re-tooted it as if it were brand new.
Nothing breaks when this happens, you just get a duplicate toot linking to the same post under its corrected URL. Harmless, but avoidable.

Mostly, with caveats. Codeberg (running Forgejo) has two CI options: Woodpecker CI, which is the more established, production-ready offering, and Forgejo Actions, which is closer to GitHub Actions in syntax but still in public alpha there and comes with tighter resource and time limits on hosted runs. Forgejo Actions supports scheduled triggers via cron, same as GitHub, so the shape of this workflow translates.

The friction is in the actions themselves. actions/checkout and actions/setup-node aren't guaranteed to exist as-is; Forgejo mirrors some GitHub Actions under its own namespace, but not the whole marketplace, and compatibility isn't guaranteed. You'd likely swap those for Forgejo-native equivalents or a plain shell script that does the checkout and Node setup manually. The script itself doesn't care where it runs, since it's just Node hitting two HTTP APIs, so the actual logic ports over unchanged. The wrapper around it is what would need adjusting.

If your instinct is host-your-own generally, this would also run fine as a plain cron job on any server with Node installed, GitHub Actions isn't a requirement, just a convenient place to run it for free without maintaining a server yourself.

entry.title: Blaugust - 10 days in
entry.summary: First time doing this whole 'blaugust' thing and it's coming along OK.

div.p: So it's day ten of Blaugust, and this is probably the longest writing streak I've ever managed. It's been genuinely challenging – but worthwhile. I've been using it to work through draft posts that have been sitting in a folder for too long, and there's something satisfying about finally getting those words out into the world.
That said, the prospect of keeping it up for 31 days is a little daunting from where I'm standing. Consider this a slightly cheeky buffer post while I buy myself some time!

One thing that has come out of this past week is a technical change to the blog worth writing about properly. I've swapped out EchoFeed (which I used to post updates on the blog over to Mastodon) as it's shutting down. I went and rebuilt my cross-posting setup directly into my existing GitHub Actions pipeline. New posts now automatically push to Mastodon and Bluesky (which is new) as part of the build process, which feels like exactly the kind of thing I should have done earlier. It's a vibe-coded solution, I used Claude, and had to do more tweaking than I'd like to admit – but it works. Building back into my current stack feels good. I know a lot of people have moved away from GitHub over the past few years, but it still gives me what I need. The yearly subscription feels well justified.

Starting Blaugust while also starting a new job was probably not the smartest timing. It's been a hectic couple of weeks, and adding a daily post commitment on top of it wasn't exactly a recipe for calm. But it's worked out better than expected, and I'm hoping to carry some of this momentum forward.

Twenty-one more days. Three more weeks. The backlog is mostly cleared now, which means the remaining posts will need to be genuinely new – and honestly, given where my work is heading at the moment, I think there's plenty to write about.
Here's to the rest of Blaugust.

entry.title: Some People Say
entry.summary: The implication of numerical weight implied by a phrase like 'some people say' is just shorthand for detecting bullshit.

div.p: I absolutely hate this phrase. I fucking loathe it. “Some people say” is shorthand in the media for here is an opinion, a hunch or a gut feeling that no one is willing to lend their name to. It’s a term that borrows substance from the implication that a numerical body of people sits behind what is being said. It’s an attempt to achieve credibility simply by implying that a number of people share an opinion. These people often don't exist, they're a device to put forward a notion or support an agenda. This use of language plays into our way of thinking that when a thing has a number attached to it, it has weight, can exert force and has presence, but it's just a trick.

This same trick applies to what Joan Westenberg explores in their post Experience Doesn't Stack The Myth of Collective Knowledge. This phenomenon of numerical presence in this piece is used as a substitute for experience and individual knowledge. - that in some way a numerical advantage of individuals trumps the expertise of an individual.

blockquote.p:
Twenty smart people, each with a year of experience, must be just as good as one person with twenty years. Right?
...
But knowledge isn’t additive. It’s not clay you pile. It’s not sandbags on a levee. It doesn’t obey volume. It compounds, condenses, crystallizes. And it does so slowly, painfully, across thousands of iterations, not from reading the same book, but from living the same questions until they evolve into different ones.

div.p: This post resonated with me as it perfectly describes my experience working in Higher Education. It happened on the first big project I was assigned. We were looking at an institutional video system, something I had initiated because I was spending vast parts of my working week converting videos. I was the expert in the room, yet when it came to choosing the video codec to use, it became a democratic process, and every member had a vote. I called this out immediately, was overruled, and then raised it with my superiors, who, on this occasion, had my back. I wouldn't be making recommendations about databases or server infrastructure, as they're outside my expertise; they should stay outside mine. I got my way, and life moved on. Thank god I was listened to and we adopted mp4 and not Windows Media Player!

My experience in higher education also shows that it's not just a numerical count that seems to trump expertise but your number in the hierarchy – those in positions above you have more weight than your expertise. Spending many years working in EdTech, I heard all kinds of pronouncements of "wisdom" from those more senior than me. That the technology would just be "plug and play", "this will be seamless", or that it will "revolutionise learning and teaching". I've watched projects fall on their arse because they didn't engage anyone with expertise or experience - of course, the consequences of those decisions were little to none - "these things can happen with radical new technologies" and "we need to fail forward".

I know that expertise is often associated with ego – and in some cases, they can go hand in hand. My counter is that "real" experts tend not to be gung-ho about things; they tend to listen more and work through the complexities. As Joan points out:

blockquote.p: One expert with twenty years doesn’t just know more facts. They see differently. They carry mental models that weren’t taught but discovered. They’ve built intuition from friction. They’ve made the same mistakes enough times to recognize them three steps before they appear. They don’t look at problems as they are but as what they become.

div.p: I'd love there to be a better counter to "some people say", but it is probably best thought of as a bullshit indicator. Once detected, there is an imperative to ask, "Which people?
