Who are they? What have they got at stake? What's their experience of this? What have they done before?" It would be great if we could acknowledge that knowledge accumulates over time. It's not the same as data or information - that's often readily available at the drop of a hat. Knowing what that data or information means, how it applies and what it doesn't show - that's far more valuable, and it should carry more weight than any number of things.

entry.title: The Answer Machine
entry.summary: There has always been a very human drive to find the Answer Machine – a device that reduces the effort required to arrive at solutions to our many problems.

div.p: There's a desire we all share as humans – the desire for answers. We're conscious, we live, we search for meaning, and that meaning often comes down to specific answers to specific questions: what is going on, and why do things happen? A lot of our time and effort on this planet goes into seeking those answers. And throughout history, there has been an enormous and recurring appeal to find an Answer Machine – a device that reduces the effort required to get there.

This innate desire goes some way toward explaining how completely we can become enraptured with whatever the Answer Machine of the moment happens to be. Once people believe they've found it, it gets embedded into every aspect of life. It becomes the mission, the thing to believe from which springs both hope and desire. Something worth fighting for, worth arguing about, worth losing for. The promise is the great payoff at the end - The Answer.
Right now, the Answer Machine is AI.

AI is perceived as the ultimate version – the one we've been building toward. The hype distils it down to exactly that: whatever problem you throw at it, AI is the solution. Climate change. Obesity. Maths homework. TPS reports. Government dysfunction. It just needs more AI. And I think this explains, at least in part, why AI feels the way it does. It taps into a millennia-long desire. A mania that feels familiar because we've been here before.
div.h3: A Short History of Answer Machines
div.p: Search was the Answer Machine of the 1990s. As the internet boomed, we needed a way to find things, and Google became that way. It wasn't overly sophisticated – you still had to click through, read the pages, find and validate the information yourself. AI feels like a better solution partly because it removes that last step. Google already scraped the data. Now it just gives you the answer, with full confidence that it's correct.

Which is, of course, where the problems start. Every Answer Machine in history has been flawed. They don't quite understand. They have the same kinds of fallibilities – hallucinations, indeterminacies, false confidence. Yet we keep going back, keep placing our faith, keep pouring money and resources into the machine and what it tells us to do.

Go back further and universities played this role. For a long time, academia was the powerhouse of answers – slower, clunkier, accessible to fewer people, but genuinely pushing innovation and making new things happen. Before that, and more controversially, religion was the primary Answer Machine. Religion gave us the rules for life, distilled lessons for what to do in certain situations, who to be, how to behave. The prophets and oracles were its more individualised expressions, but the institutional roots of religion provided the infrastructure. It's worth sitting with how well that maps onto what we're doing now.

And if we're willing to look at the fringes – at cults and conspiracy theories – we can start to understand the failure modes. These too are Answer Machines, and the reason they tend not to last is that their flaws are more obviously embedded in their structure. But the dynamics are identical: absolute fervour, total devotion, a willingness to disrupt relationships and distort your view of the world in service of the answers the machine provides. The difference between a cult and a religion is often just time and institutional legitimacy. The difference between a conspiracy theory and accepted wisdom is often just whether the Answer Machine behind it survived long enough to become popular and embedded in culture.

We're treating AI with the same fervour. Adoption without evidence. Certainty without validation. The language of hallucination is telling – it implies the problem is in our perception, not in the machine. Which is exactly how the oracles worked: if the answer didn't fit, you'd interpreted the prophecy incorrectly. AI confidently presents answers regardless of whether those answers are correct, and we've built an entire discourse around how to ask the right questions rather than whether the machine actually knows.
Every Answer Machine demands sacrifice. That's perhaps the most important thing to understand about them.

Religion has always demanded it. Cults demand it. With Google, the sacrifice was our data – our data became their oil. We submitted to being tracked and surveilled and having everything we did sold back to us as advertising. The world didn't improve because of it. The data didn't benefit humanity. It became profit for a handful of companies. We got free search in return.

AI is the same transaction at a larger scale. The capital expenditure going into AI infrastructure right now is staggering – comparable, in raw terms, to what was spent running a world war. And what is it building? Data centres. Server farms the size of hundreds of football fields, consuming power and water at rates that actively worsen the problems we're supposedly using AI to solve. Resources spent not growing food, not housing people and not maintaining the biosphere in any kind of manageable state. We are sacrificing the planet's resources on the altar of the Answer Machine, and the answers we're getting back are mostly being used to build competitive moats for a handful of corporations positioning themselves for whatever the AI wars look like in ten years.
This isn't AI for humanity. It isn't AI for the planet or the future. It's AI for profit. And we are the sacrifice.
div.h3: What the Machine Can't Tell You
div.p: The cruel irony of the Answer Machine is that the answers we most need aren't the ones it can provide. Ask anyone who has earned genuine wisdom over a long life, and they'll tell you it wasn't found in a machine, a doctrine, or a search result. It was found in relationships. In community. In paying attention to the world immediately around them. Truth of that kind isn't something you retrieve – it's something you build, slowly, through connection and presence and time.

We live in a society so oriented toward seeking alternative answers that we've lost the habit of sitting with what's actually in front of us. The Answer Machine, whatever form it takes, always promises to shortcut that process. And it always asks more than it gives.

The answers to what we seek are closer than the machine would have us believe. They're in our families and communities, in the land, in the connections we form and maintain. Not in what's ephemeral. Not in what some model can confidently generate. In what's real, and present, and ours.

entry.title: Diversity is a Superpower
entry.summary: One of the things I want to do over the next little while is start sharing solutions – things I've done to solve problems, the approaches taken, and the lessons learned. Not theory. What actually worked. So here's some thoughts on building a team.

div.p: When I worked at CSU, educational designers were school and faculty based but centrally managed. They were embedded in their own areas, responding to the specific needs of the academics they worked with. It didn't take long after I joined to realise that every single one of them had developed a completely different set of skills and approaches. On one level that was interesting. On the other hand, it meant the work had become deeply atomised. Everyone operated in their own bubble. There was collegiality and a genuine desire to do better, but the structure of the team didn't allow for it.

When I joined the University of Adelaide, I had the opportunity to build something from the ground up. One of the things I was most focused on was developing a genuine team approach to delivering learning design — not a group of individuals working in parallel, but a team that actually functioned as one.

The team I built included media developers, learning designers, and project officers. That diversity of skills created an environment where a lot of organic work developed naturally. Things got done faster because you weren't waiting for approvals or scheduling meetings to have conversations — you could stick your head over a desk and ask.

As we grew from two to six learning designers, I got to hire each person joining the team. What I was looking for wasn't just competence — I already had two accomplished learning designers as a foundation, so I could afford to take some calculated risks. What I was really looking for was diversity: different backgrounds, different strengths, different ways of seeing problems.
That turned out to be the best decision I made.

Having a diverse set of skills and perspectives ensured we had the breadth of skill and experience to deal with every situation and context. What was required was the creation of the right structures and processes for collaboration – common points of contact and shared ways of working that adapt to different contexts rather than imposing uniformity. We had to create spaces that surface the knowledge and perspective each individual brings.

Each learning designer held the lead role on specific courses, enough work to keep them fully occupied. What made the difference initially was ensuring that each team member could discuss their course and their challenges. Our meetings became spaces for conversation among team members throughout the process. Rather than meeting to discuss progress, we outsourced that to Jira; we discussed our work - shared the challenges and opportunities, asked for feedback, and sense-checked decisions.

We also developed shared artifacts that made collaboration concrete. Course maps became a common language — skeletal diagrams of an entire course that could be passed between designers, reviewed, and built on. Feedback loops became a normal part of the process because it created a point for collaboration rather than a formal checkpoint.

We also adopted an agile philosophy, which brought with it sprints, Jira, and the associated language. Of everything that came with agile, the single most valuable thing was the retrospective. Having a built-in ceremony where the team could review decisions, name what wasn't working, and actually change things, shaped the way we operated more than almost anything else.

Early on, I was fixated on consensus and getting everyone to agree before moving forward. The intention was good: I wanted the team involved in decisions so they understood the reasoning and were genuinely on board. The problem was that getting consensus was slow, and my own indecisiveness didn't help. I didn't want to be authoritarian, but consensus wasn't working either.

The answer came through stumbling across consent-based decision-making. We didn't adopt the formal process wholesale, but the core idea changed how we operated: propose a solution, get permission to proceed, then build in a review. The retrospective became the natural home for that review — a ceremony that made the whole loop work.
This became the space in which we made progress - adapting documentation and processes, tweaking styles and adding layout option, adopting best practices across the team.

The big one was two fully online programs. But it also included processes that held up through a pandemic, staffing challenges, and the friction that comes with any team of people from genuinely different disciplines. A group that knew how to co-labour – not just cooperate, but actually work together on the hard problems. Diversity, it turns out, isn't a nice-to-have for a team. It's the mechanism by which the team actually works.

At the end of last year I said farewell to my old team as we prepared for the final stage of "the merge". When I look back, it is with a sense of pride rather than sadness. The gut-feeling I had around collaboration was right. What I didn't realise was that you can't just plonk a group of diverse individuals together and expect collaboration. You have to create the environment and structure to do it. It requires action, purpose, and support to work. There is a level of infrastructure required for collaboration to occur - spaces to discuss, trust to create, debates to have, disagreements and conflicts, but also resolutions and peace. Collaboration isn't something that just happens; you have to nurture and care for it. It takes time and effort and patience, but when it all clicks – it is magic! That is the thing I miss – the magic! Knowing I had a team of the very best people to work with, and that by working together we could do anything and solve any problem. And that feeling - that's the solution for how you want to work and what you want your job to feel like.

entry.title: The Professional Toolkit
entry.summary: Can you just roll up your tools and leave any more? Some thoughts on the nature of labour and higher education.

div.p: My barber recently moved premises, set up on his own, and I found something genuinely compelling about that. The ability, as a professional, to essentially pick up your tools, find a new chair, and keep going. The skill is his. The relationship with his clients is his. The craft he's spent years developing is entirely portable. If a landlord puts the rent up, or an employer devalues his labour, he has real options. He can leave.

It got me thinking about what that actually looks like in a university context – and how unevenly that kind of portability is distributed. It also started me thinking about my new role, and what it feels like coming into somewhere new and different, even within the same organisation.

On the surface, academics seem like the university equivalent of the barber. And in some ways they are. A researcher builds a body of work that belongs to them, not the institution. Their reputation is individual and travels with them. Their relationships in their discipline usually span institutions and continents. Their publications, their intellectual contributions – these are genuinely portable in a way that most professional roles aren't. There's a reason academic recruitment looks the way it does: you're hiring a person and everything they've built, not just filling a seat.

But even this has limits. The infrastructure that supports academic work – the labs, research funding, relationships, administrative machinery that keeps everything running – none of that moves. And increasingly, the conditions under which academic work happens are so shaped by institutional systems and processes that the portability is more theoretical than real for many people working in that space.
The more interesting case, though, is that of professional staff – the people who actually run the mechanisms and systems of universities. And I include myself in this.

My role exists within a specific institutional machine, and I'd say I've become quite good at operating that machine. I understand its quirks, knowing which levers do what and in what order, but that expertise is deeply contextual to my machine. Even if another university runs what looks like the same machine, it's a different model, configured differently, embedded in a different culture, connected to different systems. The skills transfer is partial at best. It's not rolling up the tools and finding a new chair. It's starting again with a machine you've never operated, drawing on instincts developed elsewhere and hoping they're close enough.

This isn't unique to universities, or even to professional services roles. It's become the dominant shape of work across most industries – we've shifted from developing craft to developing operational knowledge of specific systems. The machine changes, the knowledge doesn't travel.

What makes this particularly interesting in a university context is the gap it creates between the two main workforces. Academics are, at least in principle, developing and owning portable human capabilities – that's more or less the point of the work. Professional staff are frequently doing the opposite: becoming more specialised, more institutionally embedded, more dependent on the specific machine they operate. The longer you stay, the better you get, and the harder it becomes to leave on your own terms.
This is the question the barber analogy keeps pushing me toward. What do you actually own, as a worker?
The barber owns the skill. It lives in his hands, his judgement, his years of practice. No employer can take that from him.
The academic, at their best, owns a body of work and the reputation that comes with it. That's real capital, even if the conditions for producing it are increasingly constrained.

The professional staff member – and I'm talking about myself here – often owns neither. What they own is deep knowledge of a specific machine in a specific place. That has real value, but it's value that mostly accrues to the institution rather than to the person. And it puts the person in a more precarious position than the income we get paid might suggest.

There's a provocation in here that I haven't fully resolved. Universities are, nominally, in the business of developing human capability – portable, transferable, genuinely owned by the person who develops it. That's the promise at the heart of the enterprise. And yet the professional workforce that makes universities function has largely been built on the opposite principle: people trained to be indispensable to a machine rather than to move independently through the world.
I don't think that's intentional. But I do think it's worth naming.

entry.title: The Politics of Care
entry.summary: More thoughts on contemporary politics and the growing sense that something is missing from what's currently on offer.

div.p: Most democratic parties are built around an underlying ideology that drives not just their appeal, but the principles guiding their decisions. Conservative politics is, at its core, about conserving the status quo – slowing change, maintaining what exists, keeping control of the conditions. That's a coherent position. Labour movements emerged as a direct counterweight, built around workers' rights at a time when labour had been so devalued it amounted to exploitation on a massive scale. They played an essential role in shifting that dynamic.

But neither has kept pace with where we actually are. Labour parties globally have drifted toward the ideological centre, adopting positions that would have been considered conservative a generation ago. Greens parties, despite the accelerating urgency of environmental collapse, have largely retreated from big-picture environmental vision into skirmishes around niche social issues. What we're left with is politics ground down into hot-button fragments – not clashes of ideology at scale, but point-scoring over small targets. The big picture has gone missing.

Adam Curtis made an observation in his recent work Shifty that keeps coming back to me: that over the past few decades, political parties of all stripes voluntarily surrendered the levers of power they once held, ceding them to the market. The result was something like a new aristocracy – not based on land or title, but on the accumulation and control of capital. Money as the organising principle of society, with politics increasingly in its service rather than the other way around.
So what's the alternative ideology? What's the rallying point?
The word I keep landing on is care.

Not care as a soft sentiment, but care as a hard political principle – the idea that the economy exists to serve people, not the other way around. This isn't a new idea, but it's one that's been systematically marginalised. The Scene on Radio series on democracy made this stark for me: the model of democratic governance, particularly in the American tradition, was never really built around 'people power'. It was built around the protection of property, those that owned could vote and participate in demorcacy. Those that were owned couldn't. While in the US it might be more explicit - property rights sit at the foundation of "Western" legal, political, and economic systems in ways that have become so naturalised we barely notice them anymore.
Property not people.

What if we inverted that? Not to attack property as such, but to subordinate it – to insist that property should serve people, that life is more important than ownership, and to build policy from that foundation upward.

The implications are significant but not radical in the way that word usually implies. Tax reform that ensures the wealthy pay in proportion to what they extract. Living wages and genuine support systems. Healthcare as a service of care rather than a commodity. Education built around human development rather than economic output. And critically, infrastructure recognised for what it actually is – the shared foundation that makes private enterprise possible at all.

For example, Amazon cannot exist without a road network. If a business benefits from public infrastructure, public systems, public education, and public order, then the question of what it contributes back isn't ideological – it's just accounting.

I think there's genuine appetite for this kind of politics. What seems to be missing is the willingness to name it clearly and build around it – to say, without apology, that empathy is not a weakness, that care is not naivety, and that the capacity to organise collectively around shared problems is one of the things humans actually do best. The alternative – every person extracting whatever they can, consequences be damned – isn't freedom. It's just exploitation with better branding.

The world is literally burning while capital flows into AI investments and data centres, away from the human and environmental systems that underpin everything else. That's not an accident; it's the logical endpoint of an ideology that puts property before people.
The question then is do we care enough to change?

entry.title: Culture is Complex
entry.summary: One of the things I keep coming back to is how poorly we understand culture as a system – and how that misunderstanding shapes the way we respond when something goes wrong.

div.p: Culture is a container word. It describes something without actually describing anything in particular. We use it to gesture at something vast and real, but the word itself gives us no purchase on what's actually going on. It names the surface without capturing what's underneath.

The metaphor I find most useful is a pond. When you sit beside one, you just see the surface – it reflects the sky, changes colour with the light, looks calm or choppy depending on the weather. But the pond isn't the surface. The pond is the ecosystem underneath: plants producing oxygen, predators and prey, nutrients cycling through waste and back into life. None of that is visible from where you're sitting. Maintaining a pond means constantly balancing competing systems you mostly can't see, and a change in one part ripples through all the others in ways that aren't always predictable.

That's how culture actually works. The media we consume, the outrage engine of social media, decades of entrenched norms around violence, the bifurcation of politics into increasingly hostile camps – none of these is the singular cause of anything. But they interact. They feed each other. They are the ecosystem beneath the surface.

Take the assassination of Charlie Kirk in 2025 as an example. In the immediate aftermath, the commentary fractured instantly into competing singular explanations – it was political violence, it was mental illness, it was a hate crime, it was inevitable, it was incomprehensible. Everyone reached for the one cause that confirmed what they already believed. But the more honest response is that multitudes can be true simultaneously. It's tragic that someone with a wife and two kids is dead. It's also true that when you make a career out of speaking hate, you are adding something to the ecosystem – and ecosystems produce outcomes that no single actor controls or intends. That's not a contradiction. That's just how complex systems behave. Separate parts can produce entirely contradictory results without ceasing to be part of the same system.

The instinct to find a silver bullet – one cause, one fix – is understandable, but it's the wrong frame. Quite often our interventions in complex systems produce the opposite effect to what we intended, because we're pushing on the surface without understanding what's underneath. That doesn't mean we do nothing. It means we stop expecting any single intervention to solve everything, and start thinking about changing conditions rather than controlling outcomes. Making certain things less likely. Adjusting incrementally. Watching how the ecosystem responds and adapting accordingly.

The pond didn't become what it is overnight. It won't become something different overnight either. But you can change what grows in it – if you're willing to work at the level of the ecosystem rather than the surface.

entry.title: Labor are the new conservatives
entry.summary: When the political party, with its roots in the labour movement, no longer represents workers' needs, what has it become? With a lack of ideas and an agenda devoid of progress and change, I'd suggest that it's now the conservative party.

div.p: The Labor Party are now the conservatives. I've been sitting with this for a big chunk of the year, turning it over and over. I keep coming back to the same conclusion: the Australian Labor Party no longer represents working people in any meaningful sense. Not in its policies, not in its priorities, and not in the people who run it.

This didn't happen in a vacuum. The Liberal Party's drift toward the hard right created a space in the centre, and Labor moved into it – partly as an electoral calculation, partly out of comfort, and partly because many of the people now running the Labor Party have more in common with the people running the Liberal Party than they do with the workers they built the party around and are supposed to represent. Both parties have been captured by the same cohort: elite university graduates, mostly with law degrees, who made the right connections, moved through the right institutions, and landed in Parliament without ever really experiencing what it means to...you know, labour. They never experienced the squeeze of living pay-check to pay-check. Never had to go on welfare when things didn't go your way. When you're earning enough to accrue a property portfolio that's always appreciating, when your income outpaces the cost of living, when your kids can move into one of the houses you already own — you're not feeling the same pressure as the people voting for you.

The evidence isn't hard to find. During a decade of housing unaffordability that has locked an entire generation out of the market, Labor offered no serious structural response. Negative gearing – one of the most straightforward levers available, a policy that actively rewards property investors at the expense of first home buyers – remains mostly untouched. Sure, it's been grandfathered since the first of July, but even with an absolute majority and mandate for change, they've still done nothing to address the fact that the remaining policy still costs the nation billions. The workers who can't afford to buy a house are still waiting. At the state level, Labor governments have gone further – actively restricting the right to strike in essential services, the most fundamental tool workers have ever had. The party of the labour movement is making it harder to organise. It would be funny if it weren't so damaging.

The Greens aren't the answer to this, they are a brake, not a vision. They're useful for moderating the worst of what the dominant parties put forward, and holding a balance of power is genuinely important – but it's not a governing alternative. There's no coherent working-class agenda coming from the Greens, no alternative economic framework, no sense of what they'd actually do with power if they had it. In a bicameral, oppositional parliament, we somehow have two major parties that agree on most significant issues and a minor party whose primary function is to make those issues slightly less bad.

Meanwhile, the Overton window keeps sliding right. The terms of political debate have shifted so far that what would have been considered mainstream Labor policy twenty years ago now reads as radical. The media landscape reflects this too – working-class voices, perspectives, and concerns are largely absent from the places where political narratives are shaped. Let's not even start on the racial makeup of the media being so far removed from reflecting society is it any wonder people are fleeing to alternatives?It's not that the workers don't exist any more ... they're still the majority of the population! They just don't have a seat at the table where the conversation happens.

And the left hasn't helped itself. Rather than forming a broad alliance, the left has splintered into a thousand unique issue-focused groups, each with its own agenda and inability to connect with others. This "identity politics" (and I want to be careful here, because I believe each individual cause is correct) has fragmented what could be a formidable political coalition into competing interest groups. When everyone identifies as something different, no one identifies with anything in common. Solidarity requires a shared stake in a shared outcome. That's hard to build when the political energy is organised around difference rather than common ground. The working class – people who work for wages, who rent, who can't absorb an unexpected bill, who are one missed pay cheque away from genuine hardship – are the majority, and yet they don't have a political home.

This is where it gets dangerous. Disaffected working-class voters don't disappear. They go somewhere, and right now that somewhere is increasingly One Nation. This is a party that has correctly identified systemic alienation and is at least talking about people who feel ignored, but it offers nothing useful in response. The appeal isn't ideological for most of these voters. It's emotional. Someone is finally angry on their behalf. That Labor has ceded this ground, that the workers' party has left working people so unrepresented that a hard right populist movement is filling the gap, is a profound failure.

So here's the call. Labor needs to reclaim its foundation before it loses the plot entirely. Not rhetorically – not another campaign about "working families" delivered by someone who hasn't missed a paycheck in a decade – but substantively. Housing policy that prioritises people over portfolios. A wage policy that actually keeps pace with the cost of living. A restored right to organise. These aren't radical asks. They're the basics. They're what the party was built to do.

If Labor won't do it, someone else needs to. A political movement genuinely organised around working-class interests, housing, wages, conditions, and the cost of living isn't a niche proposition. It's a majority proposition. The numbers are there. What's missing is the representation. The workers are the largest class in this country, and right now they are the least heard. That's not just a political problem. It's an opportunity for whoever is willing to take it seriously.

entry.title: Blaugust
entry.summary: Long time blogger, first time Blaugger

div.p: I came across this toot from Tantek yesterday (August 1st). I'd just published my July recap and been feeling quite neglectful of the blog this year. I've started cleaning up my Obsidian space and now have a folder of drafts and half-arsed, half-finished posts. There are about 27 posts in there, so I started to put that together with the Blaugust call to action, and now I'm thinking - yes, let's aim for 31 posts in a month.

So let's jump into a post on my thoughts on August itself. It's cold. As far as the Adelaide winter goes, August feels much colder, and that's because the skies clear up. Gone is the oppressive winter gloom that descends in May and lasts through July. The clouds and the rain clear up - and the sun returns (welcomed), but the clear skies mean that nights are cold. Each evening, any warmth the sun provided escapes into the night sky. The mornings aren't as dark, and the days have turned a corner, and it's darker after 5 pm now, but it's cold.

Cold on the pre-dawn dog walks and cold as soon as the sun dips below the horizon - usually when I'm walking home from the train. There are spectacular sunrises and sunsets, though – and peering out through the windows, there are blue skies and patches of sun returning to our lives. But it is cold. The sun is still too far away to really provide much warmth; it's tantalising but ultimately disappointing. There are still clouds, but the kind like the Simpsons credits, fluffy and singular rather than a singular grey mass. They zip across the sky and cast deep shadows, the light too weak to pass through. They make a walk outside a clothing challenge – leave in just a shirt, and you will freeze in the shadows, or walk in a jumper and feel yourself get a little bit too humid for comfort.
But it's change, and it marks the end of the hibernation period. Everywhere is green and damp, ready to grow when the heat returns.
PS - You can sign up for Blaugust yourself here

entry.title: July 2026
entry.summary: A new job and another ride around the sun.

div.p: July has felt fairly momentous. It started with wrapping up my old role – a couple of team lunches, some farewell drinks on a cold and cozy evening, and a fairly anticlimactic send-off from senior leadership. What I did get, and what actually mattered, were some genuine words from my team, past and present. That meant a lot.

Looking back, the biggest accomplishment in that role wasn't any single project or initiative – it was building the team itself. Bringing together people with genuinely diverse skill sets and backgrounds and creating an environment where they could actually collaborate. It was the thing I'd set myself as a challenge when I took the role at Adelaide - knowing it was a missing piece in my career path up to that point.

Before leaving, I had a chance to catch up with my new director and hear a bit about the future direction of my new role. It gave me something to chew on – what my role could look like, what I might bring to it. A good way to close one chapter and orient toward the next.

Then we had four days in Brisbane — just me, Miss A, and K — which was exactly what was needed. It's been a rough year as a family unit. Having a 14-year-old navigating change and bringing all of that home has been challenging for everyone. So having some time to decompress and just enjoy each other's company was good. We got our art and sculpture fix at GOMA and the gallery, wandered the city, and stayed in the CBD this time, which opened up parts of Brisbane I hadn't really seen before.

From Brisbane we drove up the Sunshine Coast to catch up with family — my mum, brother, sister, and their kids. We had a day at Australia Zoo, which produced a Beatles-mania moment for my nieces when we saw Bindi and Terri Irwin perform with the crocodile show. I was actually amazed that they exist as real people continuing in that job is genuinely interesting.
Then it was back on the plane, and Monday morning I rolled into the new job.

The first week was less about settling in and more about hitting the ground. I spent most of it working on an EOI to bring some business into the university, which turned out to be a pretty good way to start – it forced me to get across what we actually do and what we want to promote. In between, I started meeting the team and getting a feel for how things are set up. There's already a lot of process improvement work visible that plays naturally to my strengths.

In the middle of all of that, I had a birthday. Bought tickets to see Queens of the Stone Age and Primus at the end of the year, and had a nice dinner out with friends at a new Malaysian place. The restaurant made their own lychee cider — apparently 6%, but deceptively so. Highly recommended.
The change feels good. There's that saying that a change is as good as a holiday, but having both in the same month is probably a level up on that.

I've also been doing some reflecting on the performative side of work – what it takes to operate in large organisations, what I'm actually good at, and where I consistently fall short. I have a high pain threshold, which serves me well in a crisis but means I'm genuinely bad at noticing when things aren't working until I've absorbed more than I should. I'm also not a natural performer – I wear everything on my sleeve, which I've always thought of as a feature rather than a bug. But it's becoming clearer that a lot of organisational culture that claims to value openness is actually asking for the performance of openness, not the real thing. Something I need to sit with.

Farewell drinks and team lunches to close out the old role. Four days in Brisbane with Ms A and Mrs K — GOMA, the art gallery, city wandering and riding scooters around the gardens. Then up to Coolum for a few days and a day trip to Australia Zoo on the Sunshine Coast. It was great spending time with mum, brother, sister, and the nieces. A birthday dinner at a Hut and Soul.
The Agency Season 2 was good. Really enjoyed the story arc and evolution of Martian.
Season 3 of Buried was really interesting. It delves into the world of hare coursing (that seen from Snatch of the dogs chasing the hare).

entry.title: June 2026
entry.summary: The lows and highs of midwinter

div.p: June has been pretty up and down – but I am ending the month on a bit of a high, having accepted a new role at the university in the Learning Futures team as the Capability Development Manager. There were a few bumps along the road to getting the role – a couple of failed job applications along the way as well. The whole process made me reflect a lot on the work I've done and the things I've achieved, and think about what I need to do next. So it's awesome that an opportunity came up to move forward and pursue something new, because I was feeling trapped during those slightly darker times in the month.

Dark is definitely how most of June has felt, despite the last weekend being bright and sunny. So much of the month has felt dark and grey, and that's probably reflected my mood for the vast majority as well. It's been incredibly wet, and with our house, that also means that it's incredibly green because this is the time of the year when all the weeds decide to come up. When we bought the house, we were advised that we could either fight them or leave them. And based on my experience so far, fighting them has proved futile.

The other impact of the weather has probably been on health and fitness. The weather is not conducive to getting out much. Frankie pulled a muscle in his leg, so he had to rest and recover. I was really getting into my bike commuting – but not enough to embrace the wet or the cold with our end-of-ride facilities. So it's been fairly quiet.

This is the time to want to hibernate, but July is looking pretty good. There's a family trip away to Queensland before I start the new job. My birthday is coming up too - so I'm actually looking forward to next month.

We did head down to Victor Harbour when it was Whale Fest - didn't see any whales but did have a really good walk along the beach, talking and planning. We then continued walking from East Terrace to West Terrace in the city. The in-laws came down for a week, and Ms A had a school musical theatre performance, which was fun. Had a great dinner out at Noi while they were here.
Finished Dark Winds season 4. Really enjoyed Guy Richie's Young Sherlock series and watched Shaun of the Dead as the family movie.
The latest season of Uncover was really good - The Expert Witness. Also listened to the third season of The Bomb which was a great story of Kennedy and Kruschev.

entry.title: May 2026
entry.summary: Plenty of signal and plenty of rain.

div.p: So it's been a bit of an up-and-down month. May is traditionally when the winter really starts to kick in, and the darkness is upon us. The days are significantly shorter. The weather is definitely grey and wet, and that really does affect my mood. I'm really starting to come to terms with the fact that I am severely affected by the weather these days. So with the weather change comes more time inside, a bit of introspection, and a cleanup of the 'inside things'.

I spent a good amount of time cleaning up my Obsidian notes. Obsidian's been a my main tool for writing, working and recording things in general, and I've taken a very organic approach to working with it. I never bought into the kinds of structures I saw others using and so just went with the flow, but I think it had gone to a point where I needed to actually do a clean up and in some structure. So for all of this month, I've actually been working on updating and renovating my vault. Tweaking metadata, moving files and cleaning things up. And that's been a really good thing to actually do, and give my "second brain" a bit of a spring clean.

What I've become aware of is that I have two different versions of a lot of what I do – the blog version and the notes version, and what I really wanted was to just have a single version of the file, but copies living in two different spaces. So I've been working with Claude to clean up my data, add some functionality to 11ty, and really try to hone my tags, categories, and the organisation of files across my system.

I've also been doing this alongside building out the genesis of a portfolio. Again, working with Claude to build out the features I want in my portfolio so I can actually see and play around with it. A big part of this is developing the metadata I need to capture and determining what information about the different projects I worked on I need to be useful. It's also helped me consider the structure as well – is speaking or attending a conference a project? Or is that something else? My aim is really to chart my career over the last 20 or so years of work, because I am now of an age where I have close to 20 years of work in higher education under my belt, and a few side projects as well. It's pretty time-consuming, and sometimes I don't have the energy to do it. The big issue with the structure is now feeling settled, but I still need to actually write up all the projects, and that's hard work.

Looking back on those 20 years has been a bit of a retrospective, making me think about what I've been able to achieve and what I haven't. This has fed into a couple of job applications (internal within the university), and I am pondering the future, but through the lens of the past. When I do look back, I see plenty of achievements and an ability to get things done despite the challenges. I also recognise that it's been a while since that work was acknowledged, or since my contribution was seen as positive by leadership. The last few years, in particular, have seen a marked shift in culture, and it's not one I do well with. The period when I had creative control and a level of authority to lead is definitely over, and it's been replaced not just by a hierarchy, but by one that is completely risk-averse, to the point of being unable to proceed with anything. The days of erring on the side of action are over, and the hope of ever being agile again disappears along the axis of yet another Gantt chart.

In a somewhat ironic coincidence (given the title of my last post) - I managed to attend the Signal not Noise conference in Adelaide. This was put on by a community of Agile and Design Thinking aficionados who have also rebooted a MeetUp (remember those pre-COVID?) that I've been attending to broaden my network. I still feel on the outer – most of the people attending were in distinctly corporate roles, but the subject matter is of interest. The conference was an interesting selection of ideas. The keynote opened by introducing the concept of "synchrony", a biological phenomenon in which individuals in a group tend to synchronise aspects of their biology. With newer generations of sensors, it is now possible to map brain functions outside an MRI (by wearing a small cap full of sensors), which has opened up new kinds of tasks and situations in which we can study the brain. One of the really interesting ones is in studying groups or even pairs, and there seems to be evidence that people who know each other and have a relationship tend to show synchrony in their thoughts. You do tend to 'click' or 'vibe' or get into the flow with others! I found that really interesting. especially when applying this to a team, and a team with quite different personalities – how do you create the vibe?

There was a presentation on emotional dysregulation that used a concept similar to Myers-Briggs to discuss emotional triggers and emotional balance. While I know there are flaws with this way of thinking, I also see power in generalisations and stereotypes, and, dealing with an emotionally dysregulated 14-year-old, I am open to suggestions. We built a professional profile using AI, which was a really interesting activity. This was aimed at developing an external insight into how you are portrayed online and how you might be perceived – for me, this blog is both a blessing and a curse. My old agile coach introduced his concept of Self 2.0 - a way of positioning ourselves in a world of AI. And I wrapped up the day by listening to an application of agile methods to physical product production practices. The day had a lot jammed into it - and I did need a couple of days to process all the information. There was definitely a lot of signal.

As a family, we headed to one of the duelling Medieval Fair events in the Adelaide Hills. It was quite a wet day, but fun to see the nerds out enjoying themselves! I also headed for a night out with workmates for a birthday. We had dinner and then went to a nightclub... which wasn't my happy place - but I had a good night and plenty of laughs.

I watched Daredevil: Born Again and I don't think I care about anything Marvel any more. We finished the second season of The Pitt and then went back and watched the 3 episodes of Season 1 we missed because I thought it was just 12 episodes! We had a couple of family movies - Watching Akira and Demolition Man. Clare and I watched Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die which I quite enjoyed.

I stumbled into Stakeknife, a series about an IRA informer for the British during the troubles, and got lost in the whole thing - absolutely bingeing it over a weekend. There is something about the stories of Northern Ireland that I find captivating. It always takes me back to the lunch room in Buncrana and chatting to Danny in our break and hearing his stories of growing up in Derry. After that, I went and binged on Mark Horgan's previous podcast, Where is George Gibney?, which was another disturbing story, but one that had a powerful effect on the lives of those affected. Definitely recommend them both.

entry.title: When the Noise is the Signal
entry.summary: The media has become a noise machine. The only way to find the signal is to connect with the people on the other end.

div.p: I've always loved the signal-versus-noise framework from information theory. James Gleick's The Information was one of those books that genuinely changed how I see the world. It introduced me to the idea that the history of communication technology is essentially a long effort to improve the signal while reducing noise. The digital revolution itself was, at its core, a solution to that problem: hard-coding information in a way that was far less susceptible to degradation than analogue formats. The signal-to-noise concept helps to understand the world around us, and our information environment is in serious trouble, not because of the internet, but because of what's been done with it.

It's easy to blame the internet for the feeling many of us are experiencing, where everything has gotten louder and more chaotic. But the internet itself isn't especially noisy. The people who actually build and maintain websites – who publish things under their own name, linked to their own identity – are relatively few. If anything, that culture of independent publishing was more alive in the early 2000s than it is now. What's changed is the platform layer: the walled gardens of Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, where you can't read or contribute without being part of the platform. Alongside the digital platforms, legacy media have undergone their own transformation over the same period.

That transformation has a clear architect. Rupert Murdoch figured out, earlier than almost anyone, that noise sells. What people were actually willing to spend time and money on wasn't the signal – the authoritative, considered journalism that newspapers held up as their reason for existing – it was the tabloid stuff. The gossip, the celebrity scandal, the beef, the outrage. He shifted newspapers toward that model through the 70s and 80s, then applied the same lesson to television in the 90s and 2000s. What Murdoch pioneered was that you could build an entire media apparatus around producing noise.

The result is that our relationship with the media has inverted. Noise used to be the thing you tolerated to get to the signal. The classifieds and the ads that paid for the journalism, and so they had a place. Murdoch realised you didn't need to bother – the noise is the product. Headlines exist for their own sake. Opinion has replaced reporting. The metric is engagement, not understanding – and engagement, it turns out, is most reliably generated by things that provoke rather than inform. We see this on a weekly – or more honestly, daily – basis as the outrage machine kicks off another cycle of noise.

A recent episode of the Lamestream podcast illustrated this perfectly. A story that deserved serious treatment – an Australian citizen denied entry to the United States without a criminal record, raising real questions about what's happening to the relationship between allies – collapsed almost immediately into tabloid coverage of the person's girlfriend's opinions. That became the headline. That got repeated across the media landscape, Murdoch and non-Murdoch alike. Because that's how infected the whole ecosystem has become. It's not just the outlets that started as noise machines. It's everything now.
McLuhan said the medium is the message. I'd update that: the medium doesn't matter, there's no message anymore. No one's really trying to communicate anything.

The newspaper is devoid of news. The TV schedule is reality show, single opinions, and panel shows of opinions. We don't even watch any more - our time divided by our second screen and the show becomes background noise. The social apps present an infinite scroll – there is no end, the algorithm always has more. Engagement is the only metric that matters. Engagement? Really? Are we actually engaged at all?

And with AI, this is all going to get worse before it gets better. Generative AI is, among other things, a noise amplification machine – capable of producing plausible-sounding content at a scale and speed that makes the current environment look restrained. The signal isn't going to get easier to find.

My own media diet has drifted a long way from the algorithmic mainstream. I'm not on the major platforms. What I do have is Mastodon – non-algorithmic, heavily curated, and slow in a way I've come to appreciate. My whole approach to social media has been about controlling what I consume: unfollowing ruthlessly, treating the feed as something to be shaped rather than something that happens to you. I've found that asymmetric following is underrated – I don't need to follow everyone who follows me, and vice versa. Often, the most useful signal comes not from the original account but from someone else boosting it, which means a human has already done some curatorial work.

There are still people out there looking for a signal in the noise. And I think the way you find it is the same way it always was: through other people. Not algorithms – algorithms just increase the noise. Through actual human connection, which is what the open web, at its best, always facilitates. What made the early internet genuinely exciting wasn't the technology – it was the people behind the pages. Individuals with names and lives and ideas, linked together by genuine interest. People as people, not as sound bites and opinions – but thoughts, feelings and contradictions. With pain and sadness, regrets and joy – so much joy, enough to affect you across the wires and tendrils that connect words and minds.

If we want the signal, we have to realise that it is carried by the people. That person behind the webpage, with a life as complex as yours, trying to make sense of the same world. That's the signal we're actually looking for. And I think we have an innate capacity to tune ourselves to find it, to filter out the rest, if we're deliberate about it.
I'm hoping that capacity doesn't get drowned out entirely. But I think it's going to take some work to protect it.

entry.title: AI as UI
entry.summary: While the generative components of AI capture the headlines, perhaps the chat interface is the more interesting.

div.p: Over the past year, much of the conversation in higher education has centred on what we do about AI. I think AI has actually done a service by exposing some deep problems within the educational system. The ability of a large language model to generate plausible content that could get students a passing mark is a genuine challenge. But many of these flaws already existed. What AI has done is supercharge problems that were already there.

That said, I want to step away from the generative AI debate for a moment and consider some other use cases. Towards the end of last year, I had the opportunity to attend a few conferences and came across some examples I found genuinely compelling. Several of them centred on using the chat interface not for generation, but as navigation.

Chat as a User Interface isn't something new; what's new is that it actually works! Chatbots have been deployed before, but they were universally terrible experiences. Without sophisticated language processing, if you misspell something or phrase a question poorly, you quickly hit a dead end. That's a significant problem in a learning context, because a student doesn't necessarily know what they don't know - that's the whole point of learning!

What made the examples I saw different was the deliberate decision to constrain the AI's generative component. Rather than letting the model roam freely, these implementations used it as a tool for textual and structural analysis of source materials – essentially creating a smarter and more specific search engine. The chat interface allows students to ask questions that resemble Socratic dialogue, rather than reading through structured paragraphs of text.

When I think about what kind of learning is actually happening here, it's less innovative than it might first appear. Applying my own typology of learning to what's going on: despite the "chat" element, this isn't really discursive learning. It's not about presenting different ideas, opinions, or competing positions. In fact, most of the examples I saw actively tried to prevent that; they wanted the AI to stay anchored to the source content and not drift into generative territory. What this amounts to is a new way of accessing information, not a new form of learning itself. So, while on the surface it appears to be a discussion, it masquerades as assimilative.

This reminded me of an argument from human-computer interaction that most of what we call "interaction" — a click event, for instance — isn't really interaction at all. It's simply navigation. And that's where I land on chat in this particular context: the AI becomes the UI – the user interface through which we access content. Using the chat is simply the same as clicking next.

That framing matters because it shifts the conversation. We move away from the grandiose promises of AI and towards something more modest and more useful: an evolution of the user interface. Like every interface evolution before it, this one comes with both gains and losses.

The most obvious recent parallel is the shift from mechanical interfaces to touchscreens. Touch was a genuine breakthrough for visual navigation – panning, pinching, and zooming through a map on a mobile device feels completely natural in a way that using a mouse never did. But text on a touchscreen is a different story. Every slight movement triggers a scroll or an accidental text selection. There's no cursor to orient yourself with, and editing text is a constant source of frustration. Anyone who has spent time in the Kindle Paperwhite's comments section knows there are hundreds of requests to bring back physical buttons. The interface that's brilliant for one task can be actively hostile for another.

AI as UI is no different. There are contexts where I can see it being genuinely powerful – legal documentation, for instance, where navigating dense text with a traditional interface is painful, and being able to ask direct questions could be a real improvement. For review and study – generating practice questions, finding answers to specific queries – I can see clear value. These are tasks that play to what large language models are actually good at: textual analysis and retrieval.

But for first encounters with new material, the case is much weaker. Text structured as a book or a chapter isn't just a container for information – it has a structure, a narrative, a sequence, and a flow that are deliberately designed to develop understanding. Concepts build on each other. The structure is part of the pedagogy. Replacing that with a chat interface, where a novice has to know what questions to ask before they even understand the terrain, doesn't remove friction – it just relocates it to a more dangerous place.

So where does that leave us? AI as UI is real, and it's new – but it's just a new user interface, not a revolution in learning. And like every interface before it, it will be genuinely useful in some contexts and actively counterproductive in others. The problem is that we don't yet have enough evidence to reliably distinguish between the two. We're in the middle of a hype cycle, and higher education has a long history of chasing the next medium as the thing that will finally replace or transform teaching, only to discover that the new medium works brilliantly in some situations but not at all in others.

The answer isn't to dismiss AI, nor to adopt it wholesale. It's about thoughtfully picking the right interface for the right situation — and remembering that no UI, however elegant, works well for everything.

entry.title: Why the Canvas hack was innevitable
entry.summary: While the news focuses on the hack, I wish we'd talk about the decision-making that made this thing an inevitability.

div.p: The news this week is full of stories about universities going offline after Instructure, the company behind the Canvas learning management system, was taken down by a cyberattack, shutting down LMS access for staff and students at institutions around the world.

I don't want to talk about the hack itself. I want to talk about the management decisions that got us to this point, and why this outcome was predictable — and why it's not going to change anytime soon.

The underlying problem comes down to how IT management conceptualises its own problem space. Drawing on the Cynefin framework, IT departments have largely settled on viewing themselves as operating in a complicated space: lots of interconnecting parts, but ultimately knowable and controllable with the right expertise and processes in place. That framing might have made sense when IT was contained to both a location and an appliance-based function.
The internet made it obsolete – but the model never got updated.

We moved from individual machines to networks of machines, then to networks upon networks. At that point, you're no longer managing a set of appliances — you're operating in a complex environment, one where unexpected events aren't anomalies to be prevented but inevitable features and effects. The management models didn't follow. The assumption that a five-nines uptime contract guarantees availability still makes sense for a single appliance. It makes no sense when multiple systems all depend on the same infrastructure. When AWS goes down, everything built on AWS goes down with it, often in cascading, self-reinforcing ways, because interdependent components can't resolve each other's failures.

Rather than build and manage with complexity in mind, adding in redundancies and reducing dependencies, the complicated mindset has led us to a point where single points of failure are baked into the system.

That's what we've seen with Canvas. A single point of failure brought down everything built around it, despite every institution presumably holding its contractual uptime guarantees. These weren't predictable operating failures; they were unanticipated events, and complicated paradigm systems cannot account for the unknown.

This is the accumulated result of more than fifteen years of the same management thinking repeating across institutions globally. They centralised onto AWS and equivalent virtual infrastructure because keeping it local was hard. We outsourced to external vendors. We decommissioned local server capacity and stopped local development because they were too hard (and because the consultants said so). We built a thoroughly networked world while retaining management approaches designed for a pre-networked one.

The over-reliance on the LMS as a centralised hub made this worse. The LMS was never actually good – it's a conflation of different systems and functions whose main virtue was simply aggregating them into a single place. That design pushes everything into one pathway rather than allowing the kind of interoperability a complex environment actually requires. And when the decree from management increasingly mandates that all core systems must be off-the-shelf products from established vendors (a policy that sounds like sensible risk mitigation) the result is that all your vendors share the same infrastructural single point of failure. When Canvas went down, it took every system routed through it with it. The entirety of learning and teaching functions, offline, simultaneously.

The concept of anti-fragile systems points toward a better approach. In a complex environment, redundancy isn't a luxury — it's a design requirement. A mirrored Canvas installation on local infrastructure, switchable via a load balancer, would have directly addressed this scenario. Canvas is open source, so replication was always feasible. Even mirroring to a separate AWS instance would have provided meaningful resilience. The cost is real, but so is the cost of multi-day outages across entire university systems. For infrastructure this critical, the case is straightforward.

There are of course, other models we could have adopted instead of the LMS. What I fear is that the post-mortem won't go there. The analysis, if it happens seriously, will focus on how the attackers got in – not on the management frameworks that made the damage this extensive. In a complex system, preventing every future attack is not a realistic goal. Designing for resilience when attacks succeed is.
The writing has been on the wall for a long time. I hope this is the moment that makes people ask not just "how did this happen?", but "why were we so exposed when it did?".

entry.title: April 2026
entry.summary: April's been another great month. Everything just seems to feel stable at the moment.

div.p: The good vibes are probably due to my health. I'm feeling good - much better than before. At the start of the year, I got put on statins, and while they had a great effect on my cholesterol, I'm one of those people who reacts to them poorly. Since coming off those, I feel a lot better. It probably wasn't something I noticed at the time, but there was definitely a gradual degradation in my energy levels.

That's also been helped by the weekly rides into work. Adding a minimum of 35 kilometres of cycling into my week has had a good effect – probably more on my mental state than physical, to be honest. The last couple of rides I've used the ebike functionality a lot less, basically pedalling in on the lowest levels of assistance and most of the way home as well, only switching to full assist to get up The Hill. I've also changed my route a little and am now going to and from work the same way – down Shepherd's Hill on the mountain bike trails, and the same loop back up on the return. It's a more direct route home and I don't have to navigate the back streets or main roads. We've switched back to standard time, so I can feel the days shortening. I need to leave a little earlier on ride days, otherwise I end up in the dark.

From the work front, things are kicking in. The new team is coming together, but we're mostly just getting to know each other at this point – I'm keeping it organic rather than pushing hard. At the same time, I'm starting to see some of the future work on the horizon, and be involved in some of that planning for that has been good.

I've also had more time to do my own thing. I pushed a couple of posts about Bloom'sI put together some resources to share with colleagues, and put out a call for feedback, which I've now received. So the next step is to pull all of that together and work out the best way to get it out into the world.

The other side project I've finally pulled my finger out and made progress on is a portfolio site. I've been going back through my career and pulling together a fairly substantial collection of projects, events, presentations, and initiatives. It's been good to reminisce about some of the happier times, career-wise. What strikes me is how much more open and outward-facing that work was. Since moving to Adelaide, a lot of my work has been institutional and inward-looking, and then COVID made that even more the case. Looking at it all in totality, that seems to be an anomaly and while it hasn't gone back to where it was things have improved. It's got me thinking about what the next challenges and areas I want to get into actually are.

One other thing this month: I've been properly exploring AI tools in a more considered way. Generative AI hasn't interested me much — generating content isn't something I want to hand off to anyone else, it's something I actually enjoy. But a lot of my work is scattered across different file systems, cloud storage, and file types, so using AI tools to handle some administrative tasks has been eye-opening. What I've found genuinely useful is feeding documentation from past projects into a large language model and getting back something I can edit, rather than spending hours writing it from scratch. Because the original words were mine, the end result still feels like me. The editing process smooths over the rough edges, and it still reads the way I'd write it.

I've also had a few "I wonder if this is possible" moments. One was taking a folder of Markdown files and asking whether a network graph could be generated from the front matter. Within five or six prompts, I had a usable prototype. It's not production-ready, but seeing that ability to quickly get to an MVP or proof of concept is genuinely powerful. It's an augmentation tool more than anything else – I can write scripts and code, but getting something to work would take hours or days. Being able to iterate quickly toward something refined suits the way I like to work.

I've focused almost entirely on Claude, mainly because the interactions feel more grown-up. The few times I've tried ChatGPT, it's felt like talking to a teenager – verbose responses full of emojis and saccharine verbiage, which is off-putting. I've also been reading a lot of Doug Belshaw's work on what he's been making with AI tools, which has been useful context. My use of these tools differs from what the AI companies are predicting, and it hasn't changed my view on the over-emphatic "this is going to change the world" outlook. I see a niche for the technology, but that's about it. A lot of what I'm actually doing is getting it to write bash scripts, run grep commands, manipulate files, and do the kind of administrative work that's tedious rather than meaningful. That's where it earns its keep.

Had a couple of nice meals out - Sri Lankan at Taprobane, pizza at One Sneaky Cheetah, hot chips at Chicken Chef and Mexican at Que Onda Wey. Niece and sister-in-law came to Adelaide and spent a week over the holidays, which was nice. Ms A went over to spend time with Nanna and mum came back and hung out with us for a few more days. I took time off from work to hang out – so we ended up just going to nice places to eat and drink.

Finished Paradise — can't say I'm thrilled with the second season. Watched it mainly to see where the story arc went, not sure I'll go back for more. Currently watching the second season of The Pitt. We also had a couple of movie nights as a family and watched The Prestige and Hot Fuzz, which was great fun.

The podcast Everything is Fake by Jamie Bartlett was really good. I'd like to go back and re-listen to the whole thing in one go — I was following it week to week, and the threaded narrative across episodes would work better heard in sequence. It pulls together a lot of threads that have been on my radar — kayfabe, AI, and how those ideas connect.

entry.title: All in the Verbs
entry.summary: Continuing on my work on a three-dimensional approach to Blooms – time to tackle the verbs.

div.p: At work, I've started to be involved in developing a process for program design. I am particularly interested in thinking through the tools, techniques, and approaches that make for genuinely good learning experience design. A central piece of that work are the learning outcomes: what students are doing across the program and within each individual course. This is a real opportunity to expand constructive alignment beyond a box-ticking exercise and to use it more as a strategic approach to clearly thread multiple components of the broader student experience through an entire program, scaffolded across courses.

When I started this, I didn't want to just continue with the formulaic approach to program learning outcomes. A critical part of that approach are the verbs, and as I mentioned in my last post, the current approach to learning outcomes and verb selection are structured around Bloom's cognitive dimension alone. The reality is that other dimensions exist — they just haven't been developed with the same rigour or consistency. In that last post, I started sketching those other dimensions out further. Building on existing work, but bringing a more structured and nuanced approach – making sure there are equivalent levels across each dimension, and starting to think through what is distinctive about each level and each domain.

When it comes to actually writing outcomes, though, it always comes back to the verbs. So one of the things I've been most keen to develop is a comprehensive verb list that works across all three domains — cognitive, affective, and operative — at each of the six levels.

Doing this work has been genuinely interesting. I already had a collection of verb lists I'd used as tools in previous projects, so part of the task was to consolidate them, but I also looked more broadly at what others have done, and tried to synthesise it into a coherent suite of verbs that sits consistently across the levels.

One of the more interesting realisations along the way was that some verbs are genuinely shared across dimensions. Take identify — cognitively, you might identify a pattern; affectively, you might identify the emotions present in a situation; operatively, you might identify what movements are being made in a physical space. The verb holds across all three. But at the same time, some verbs clearly belong more naturally within a specific dimension. And there's a sequencing dimension too: a verb that's standard practice within one domain at an early level might become a shared, cross-domain expectation at a higher level.

What I'm really trying to achieve is a more three-dimensional version of Bloom's. Learning has height, breadth, and width – but the affective and operative components have often been lost. These are often dismissed as "soft skills" or treated as trade-specific concerns, but they matter deeply in higher education. Higher education that includes vocational training and degrees in which cognitive, affective, and operative development are genuinely intertwined. Think about social work or nursing: those programs aren't just about building knowledge. The affective dimension, how you engage with patients and clients, and the operative dimension, how you hold yourself, how you carry out specific procedures, are core to what it means to be competent in those fields. We need to be capturing that, but also extending our thinking beyond cognitive and what students know, to what they can do and who they can be.

So, here's the verb list. I'm still working through how best to share these kinds of resources, but for now this feels like the right move — put it out there and see what people do with it. If you already have a verb list you work from, there might be things here worth adopting. Keen to hear your feedback.

entry.title: To the Dark Side
entry.summary: Tweaking the website - adding a dark mode and moving CSS to more modern and vanilla.

div.p: If you've got dark-mode enabled on your system or browser ,you might be seeing the website differently than normal. I've been mucking around as a way of learning some of the newer CSS and what's possible these days. One of the things I've been keen on is moving to a more "vanilla" approach to my websites – less reliance on frameworks, addons and plugins. So I've been trying to suss out what you can do these days with just plain old vanilla CSS.

As a designer, one of the things that I've relied heavily on in the past has been SASSto handle the grunt work of creating colour systems - all of the darker and lighter tones for each of the available colours in your palette. That can be done now using the native colour-mixing that's available in CSS. To complement that, I've been looking into making more "colourful" yet accessible use of colour across my sites. I love colour - huge, big, blocky chunks of it - and often the more eye-wateringly lush and juicy the better. I started this by updating the colours I used on the Learning Types site. One of the tricky things in a colour system is tachievingconsistency across the range. If you use yellow , the palette quickly becomesmuddied into poo-brown. In steps the OKLCH for creating my colour system.

There are a great number of colour systems – ways of codifying the hues, tones, lightness and darkness of the colours we see. Many on the web are used to the hex-codes like #ff0e69 and #ffae2c you see around the place. You might be familiar with RGBA where you can assign values to the red, green, blue and alpha (transparency) channels. Theres HSL, which does appear on this very website - which is your Hue, Saturation and Lightness. OKLCH is one of those - you define the values for the Lightness, Chroma and Hue. This is all nicely explained on OKLCH in CSS: why we moved from RGB and HSL:

blockquote.p: oklch() is a new way to define CSS colors. In oklch(L C H) or oklch(L C H / a), each item corresponds as follows:

ul.li: L is perceived lightness (0-1). “Perceived” means that it has consistent lightness for our eyes, unlike L in hsl().
C is chroma, from gray to the most saturated color.
H is the hue angle (0-360).
a is opacity (0-1 or 0-100%).

div.p: The big thing for me was this idea of "perceived" - especially because I'd been using darken() and lighten in Sass and while they might be mathematically correct, there was alway a lot of tonal differences across the colour palette. OKLCH improves that quite a bit, and while I still might tinker, it's reduced the massive variations I am used to.

So I wanted an excuse to explore OKLCH, but also some of the new variables and functions possible in CSS. Down the rabbit hole I went, but what I wanted to share was where I ended up. I've now built a colour system I am happy with – I haven't applied it to anything yet, but I've started incorporating it here. What I did was break down my OKLCH into its constituent parts.
For example I've tweaked the colour palette here to use a tint of my Soulyellow:
These are now CSS variables that I can use. So I plug them into a repeatable palette:

img.alt: What the above code looks like

div.p: And now I have a full palette for those colours. I'm using the calc function to change the hue and chroma across the range to provide a better spread and consistency alongside the other colours in the palette.
I mean – look at those beauties!! Look at the consistency across each level!
The other nifty CSS feature I've started adding to the site is a light-darkfunction. So instead of color[1] having a single assigned value, you can have one colour for light mode and one for dark.
So the background of this page element is written

Now for the site, I am still using the 11ty Rocks Sass + LightningCSS which I found out does some nifty backwards compatible tweakery, so your source code might not show that – but that's what I write. And it just works!

So I spent last night and this morning tweaking things across the site to make dark mode work. There are a few bits I need to work on (and if you see them let me know!) but I'm well underway on making the site more Dark Friendly.

li.p: I am sticking to the American spelling as it's part of the mental model I've had to build to work on the web all these years and finding errors in my code because I've tried to spell colour correctly. ↩︎

entry.title: March 2026
entry.summary: Mad March has been, genuinely, a good month.

div.p: March in Adelaide is what the locals call Mad March — all the festivals descend at once. Fringe, the more highbrow arts festivals, WOMAD – all of it and at the same time. It's also the city at its most livable – days still warm, nights just tipping into cooler territory — perfect for sitting out under the stars with a glass of wine and enjoying the gardens.

We took full advantage, catching a bunch of comedians and soaking up the Fringe. Still haven't made it to Cabaret — honestly, it's not something I grew up with in Wagga Wagga, so I've never quite known what to make of it. Maybe that's next year's experiment.

The bigger win this month has been the bike. Riding has started to feel like sustainable exercise — physically and mentally.
